Then the bow window of Fenn's is ahead, bolts of cloth and the green velvet in the light, and you push the door open. Ida Fenn sits at the window with her sewing and a mouthful of pins.

turns.do: I set my needle case on the window seat, give the rose at my collar a pat, and say, "Good afternoon, Mistress Fenn! Here I am as promised, and with nothing in my pocket but hope. Name me your seams and your price before I thread a single needle, and I'll make them neater than yesterday's, if you can believe it. And do tell me the ribbon still suits me in daylight."
turns.journal: I've not a penny left, and Ida's basket is the surest work in town, but she'll not have another night of my stitching for nothing, so the price comes first this time. I'm working toward a full pocket again and a place at this window, and one day that green velvet.
turns.outcome: done asked Ida the seams and price
turns.story:
You set your needle case on the window seat and give the rose at your collar a pat. "Good afternoon, Mistress Fenn! Here I am as promised, and with nothing in my pocket but hope. Name me your seams and your price before I thread a single needle, and I'll make them neater than yesterday's, if you can believe it. And do tell me the ribbon still suits me in daylight."

Ida Fenn looks up over her pins, her eyes going briefly to your collar and then to the ribbon.

Ida: "Hemming and seaming at the window, Marigold, a penny or two, and that's paid when the spell is done, not after. Neat, mind. The ribbon sits well enough in daylight; it would sit better if the rose were pinned an inch higher."

The afternoon light lies warm across the bolts of cloth, and the window seat waits beside her.

turns.do: I move the rose an inch higher, just as she said, and pat it. "There, Mistress Fenn, an inch higher, you were quite right." Then I pick up my needle case. "Now, which piece is it to be tonight, and is it one penny or two? Name it and I'll sit right here and have it done before the lamp wants trimming, and I won't touch a stitch more than you ask."
turns.journal: I've not a penny to my name and night's coming on, and I'll want stew and a bed, so work agreed and paid for comes before anything else. I moved the ribbon because she noticed it, and I'd like her to notice me. I'm working toward a pocket that jingles and a name at this window, and one day that green velvet.
turns.outcome: done sewing for a penny
turns.story:
You move the rose an inch higher in the bow window and pat it flat.

Marigold: "There, Mistress Fenn, an inch higher, you were quite right."

You pick up your needle case and ask which piece it is to be tonight, and whether it's one penny or two, promising not a stitch more than she asks.

Ida takes the pins from her mouth and hands you a bundle of hems from the counter, looking over her spectacles. You settle at the window and sew as the lamplight yellows. The seams come out straight and small, and Ida runs a thumb along the last one and nods.

Ida: "Neat enough. A penny."

She counts it into your palm. Beyond the bow window the evening goes grey over the Market Square, and the velvet gleams green in the lamplight.

turns.do: I tuck the penny away and give the rose a pat. "Goodness, listen to that rain, Mistress Fenn, it's a positively sodden sort of night! Tom wants two pennies for a bed and I've only the one. Have you another bundle, just one, at a penny, named now before I thread a thing? I'll have it done neat before the lamp's half down."
turns.journal: A bed's two pennies and I'll not beg Tom for it, so one more agreed spell at Ida's window is the honest way to a dry night. I'm getting the price named first every time now, and I'm building toward a jingling pocket, a name at this window, and one day that green velvet.
turns.outcome: out_of_reach another paid bundle at Ida's tonight
turns.story:
You tuck the penny away and give the rose a pat. The rain ticks at the bow window, and the lamp throws a warm square over the bolts of cloth. You tell Ida it's a positively sodden sort of night, that Tom wants two pennies for a bed and you've only the one, and ask whether she has another bundle, just one, at a penny, named now before you thread a thing.

Ida: "No, Marigold." She doesn't lift her eyes from her seam, and the pins in her mouth make it precise. "There's no more plain sewing wanted of you tonight. What was wanted is done."

The lamp hisses faintly. The needle case sits in your hand, the shop's quiet around you, and Ida's thread goes on drawing through the cloth.

turns.do: I give Ida a little bow. "Good morning, Mistress Fenn! It's market day, so I'll go and try my luck among the stalls, but I'll be back by noon if you've a seam to name." Then I sweep out into the square, lay my penny on Bet's stall for a loaf, and while I eat I call out over the carts: "Hems, collars, mending! Torn in the ford or the barley field? Marigold Thimble, the girl with the rose ribbon, a penny a piece, price agreed before I thread a thing!"
turns.journal: Ida told me plain there was nothing more wanted, and I'll not stand in her shop begging like a limp bit of muslin. Market day brings the whole town to the square, so I'll fill my stomach and show my ribbon and my needle to all of them at once. I'm working toward my own trade, a jingling pocket, and one day that green velvet.
turns.outcome: partly bread eaten, called for sewing; no customer yet
turns.story:
You give Ida a little bow and tell her it's market day, that you'll try your luck among the stalls but be back by noon if she has a seam to name. Then you sweep out of the shop into the square, where the carts are drawn up along one side and Ned Pike has his stall laid out by the pump.

You lay your penny on Bet Lamb's stall and take a loaf, and eat it standing there. Then you call out over the carts: Hems, collars, mending! Torn in the ford or the barley field? Marigold Thimble, the girl with the rose ribbon, a penny a piece, price agreed before you thread a thing!

The square carries on around you, with the pump dripping and the hammering loud from the smithy, and Bet and Ned both within earshot.

turns.do: I sweep over to Ned's stall and run a finger along his heap of seconds. "Goodness, Master Pike, what a treasure-heap! Though this sleeve's come away and that hem's hanging like a wet dishrag. Folk pay double for a second that looks like a first, you know. I'll mend any piece you pick at a penny apiece, sitting right here by the pump where everyone can watch. Name me which ones and I'll not thread a stitch more." Then I pat the rose at my collar and wait for him to tell me it's pretty.
turns.journal: Ida has nothing for me, and Ned's stall is full of things a needle could make worth more to him, so this is the quickest honest way to two pennies and a bed. I'm working toward a trade of my own beyond Ida's window, with folk all over the square knowing the girl with the rose ribbon.
turns.outcome: not_there paid mending work from Ned
turns.story:
You cross the damp cobbles to Ned Pike's horse blanket by the pump, where the cracked crocks, odd buttons and the dented lantern lie in their heap. You run a finger along the seconds and say your piece about the torn sleeve, the hanging hem, and a penny apiece, here by the pump where everyone can watch. Then you pat the rose at your collar.

Ned: "Mend 'em?" Ned laughs, quick and thin, and tips his battered hat back. "My friend, between you and me, folk who buy off a blanket don't ask after hems. A torn sleeve sells for what a sewn one sells for, and I'd be robbed to pay for it. No, no. Ribbon's a penny, lantern's a penny, and I'm already ruined by that."

His eyes slide past you to a woman looking over the cheeses at the nearest cart. Around the pump, the market goes on with its calling and its bargaining, and your needle case is still at your side.

turns.do: I pat the rose at my collar, call "Good evening, Bet love, Master Pike!" and sweep east into the Wheatsheaf after the reeve. "Mistress Pollard! Goodness, your bridge hands must be tearing their sleeves to ribbons on those timbers. I'm Marigold Thimble, the girl with the rose. I'll mend for them at a penny a piece, and you'll name which pieces before I thread a single stitch. Have you a torn coat or two I might start on tonight?"
turns.journal: Ned won't pay for mending and Ida has nothing more for me, but the reeve has a whole crew of men wearing their clothes through at the bridge, and she has the purse besides. I'll have the price named first, as always, and I'm working toward two pennies for a bed tonight and a trade folk come looking for.
turns.outcome: refused Agnes would not commission mending
turns.story:
You pat the rose at your collar and call a good evening to Bet and Master Pike, then cross the square and push in at the Wheatsheaf's door. The taproom is warm and loud with talk of the flood and the barley, and Agnes is there.

Marigold: "Mistress Pollard! Goodness, your bridge hands must be tearing their sleeves to ribbons on those timbers. I'm Marigold Thimble, the girl with the rose. I'll mend for them at a penny a piece, and you'll name which pieces before I thread a single stitch. Have you a torn coat or two I might start on tonight?"

Agnes: "Well, then, Marigold. I've no coats to give you, and they're not mine to give. They belong to the men on the bridge. The town's cash tin is nearly empty, so I can't pay for mending either." She nods toward the door. "If the men want stitching, they can strike that bargain with you themselves. If you'd rather put your back into the bridge work, I pay in hand at the end of each spell."

The fire pops at the far end of the room. Your needle case is still at your side.

turns.do: I sweep up to the bar and give the rose at my collar a pat. "Master Harrow, goodness, what a sodden, mud-hemmed sort of night! I've not a penny tonight, but I've a needle that Mistress Fenn calls neat. Have you sheets fraying at the hem, or an apron, or a cuff gone thin? Name me the pieces, and I'll do them neat and not a stitch more, if you'll call it square for a bed tonight."
turns.journal: Tom was kind to me my first night, and a bed is what I want most, so a straight trade with him is quicker than coaxing pennies out of carters who won't part with them before supper. I'll have the work named before I thread a thing, the way I've learned. I'm working toward a dry night, a name for good mending all over town, and one day that green velvet.
turns.outcome: refused mending traded for a bed
turns.story:
You sweep up to the bar with the rose pat-patted at your collar, and tell Tom Harrow what a sodden, mud-hemmed night it is. You've not a penny, you say, but you've a needle Mistress Fenn calls neat: any sheets frayed at the hem, an apron, a cuff gone thin? Name the pieces, and you'll do them neat and not a stitch more, if he'll call it square for a bed.

Tom: "Well now, Marigold," he says, rubbing his cloth along the bar and not for a moment still. "A bed's two pennies, friend, paid when you turn in, and that's the long and short of it. Sheets I've got, and I'll not pretend they're whole, but it's pots that drown me. The scullery's piled to the rafters. Wash them and I'll pay you for it, and throw in your supper besides."

Behind him the scullery door stands ajar on steam and the clatter of crockery. Carters murmur over their mugs, and the fire pops at the far end of the taproom.

turns.do: I lean on the bar and give the rose a pat. "Master Harrow, you offered me your pots last night, and goodness, I've been sorry ever since I let Dilly have them. I'll take them this morning, if they're still wanting. Name me the pay first, pennies and the supper both, and I'll have them gleaming. Though I'll do it singing, mind, with the door open so you can hear."
turns.journal: Pots are drab, sudsy work and not at all what my needle's for, but I'm hollow and dropping on my feet, and Tom's offer was a kind one, with supper thrown in. I'll have the price named first, the way I've learned, and I'm working toward a full stomach, a proper bed tonight, and pennies enough to keep going till Ida wants me again.
turns.outcome: failed washed Tom's pots; the work went wrong, no pay
turns.story:
You lean on the bar, give the rose a pat, and tell Tom you'll take his pots this morning if they're still wanting, pennies and supper both, and that you'll do it singing with the door open.

Tom: "Pots are always wanting, friend! A few pennies for a clean stack, and your supper with it, if they come out right." He jerks his thumb at the steamy door behind the bar.

You go through to the scullery and set to, singing as promised. The stack is tall, the water is greasy, and the scrubbing goes badly. Pots slip, the crust won't shift, and when you carry the first lot out Tom looks them over and shakes his head. The work has gone wrong, and there is nothing for you this time.

The taproom hums with the carters and the talk of the flood, and the pots are still stacked and waiting behind you.

turns.do: I leave the pots with a sigh and sweep over to Wat's table, patting the rose. "Master Birch, goodness, a whole harvest in that coat and it shows. That cuff's gone thin as cheesecloth and there's a rent at the elbow. I'm Marigold Thimble, neat hems by Mistress Fenn's own word. A penny for the elbow, a penny for the cuff, named now, and I'll sit right here and do them while you eat. You needn't pay a thing till you've seen them done."
turns.journal: The pots beat me, and I'll not stand dripping in Tom's scullery while a man in a torn harvest coat sits ten steps away. Wat won't part with a penny before he's heard the price, so I've given it to him plainly and let him pay after. I'm working toward supper and a bed tonight, and a name for mending that goes beyond Ida's window.
turns.outcome: partly Wat accepts the elbow only, pays when it's done
turns.story:
You leave the pots and cross the taproom to Wat Birch's table, patting the rose at your collar, and name your price: a penny for the elbow, a penny for the cuff, and nothing owed till he has seen the work.

Wat: "Well now, friend, that's kindly said, and I reckon the coat's seen better harvests than this one." He glances at the cuff and turns it over once. "Two pennies, though. I count twice before I spend once, and I've not yet a day's work nor a bed to my name. If you'll sit and do the elbow only, and I pay when it's done and I've seen it, I reckon that'd suit."

The afternoon wind rattles the door to the square. Wat waits, coat turned toward you, for your answer.

turns.do: "Done, Master Birch, the elbow only, a penny when you've seen it. Not a stitch more, I promise." I settle beside him near the fire, thread my needle where the whole room can watch, and talk him through every stitch as I close that rent small and straight. Then I hand it back, pat the rose, and wait for him to say it's neat.
turns.journal: It's a price named plain and a man willing, which is more than I've had all day, and a penny in hand beats a pot I might scrub wrong again. Stitching it by the fire lets the whole taproom see what my needle can do. I'm working toward supper, a bed, and my own name for good mending.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
"Done, Master Birch, the elbow only, a penny when you've seen it. Not a stitch more, I promise." You settle beside Wat near the fire, thread your needle where the whole taproom can watch, and talk him through every stitch as you close the rent small and straight. Then you hand the coat back, pat the rose, and wait.

Wat Birch turns the elbow over in the firelight and runs a thumb along the seam. He grins, slow.

Wat: "Well now, that's neat as you like, friend. Small and straight, and I reckon it'll hold through the whole cutting." He counts a penny into your palm and peers at it once more before letting go. "There's an honest penny for honest work."

The penny is warm from his hand. Tom is wiping down the bar nearby, and the stew pot steams behind him.

turns.do: I tuck Wat's penny away, pat the rose, and sweep over to Abel Tash. "Master Tash, goodness, you've been stranded here so long your coat's gone thin as gauze at the pocket! You saw what I did for Master Birch's elbow. Name me one tear, a penny for it, paid when you've seen it done, and I'll sew it right here by the fire, not a stitch more."
turns.journal: Robin's only got a penny he needs for his own bed, and Wat's already told me he counts twice, but Abel's watched me sew the whole evening and hasn't been asked yet. One more penny makes two, and that's a bed, and I'm so tired I could fold up like a bolt of muslin. I'm working toward a proper night's sleep and a name for good mending all over this taproom.
turns.outcome: refused Abel's penny for sewing
turns.story:
You tuck Wat's penny away, pat the rose, and sweep across the taproom to Abel Tash, who sits thick-necked over his mug with the smell of horse on his coat. You tell him how thin his coat has gone at the pocket, and offer to sew one tear for a penny, paid once he has seen it done, not a stitch more.

Abel: "Hark at her," he says, loud and sneering, a jerk of his whip-scarred cheek. "My lady wants coin for a needle! Strangers on the bridge wages, strangers in my pocket. Sew your own coat, my lady. I'll not pay a penny to be stitched."

A few carters laugh into their mugs. The fire pops at the far end, and the stair at the back leads up to the beds.

turns.do: I give the rose a pat, call "Good morning, Master Harrow, Master Birch, do tell everyone whose needle mended that elbow!", and sweep out west to the square. I give Bet my penny for a loaf, and between bites I stand by the notice board and sing out, "Neat mending, a penny a tear, price named first and paid when you've seen it! Ask Master Birch!"
turns.journal: I'm too hollow to sew a straight seam, so the loaf comes first, and the square is where Dunn's idle hands will be walking past, with Wat's elbow doing my crying-up for me. I'm working toward two pennies by nightfall for a proper bed, and a name for my needle all over Wendleford.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
You call a good morning across the Wheatsheaf taproom, asking Master Harrow and Master Birch to tell everyone whose needle mended that elbow, and step out west into the square. The cobbles are still damp in the low corners; Robin Hale is standing there.

At Bet Lamb's stall you hand over your last penny and take a loaf. You eat it between bites, there by the stall, and the hollow in you eases.

Then, by the notice board under its little slate roof, you sing out: "Neat mending, a penny a tear, price named first and paid when you've seen it! Ask Master Birch!" The board holds the reeve's notices and Ida Fenn's call for plain sewing, nothing of yours yet. Your purse is empty and the morning is just begun.

turns.do: I give the rose a pat, wave to Bet, and sweep northeast to Fenn's. "Mistress Fenn, goodness, your notice is still up in the square, so I've come to see if the rain's brought you fresh hems. Name me the pieces and the price first, the way we agreed, and I'll sit in your window and do them neat as you like."
turns.journal: Ida's notice is still pinned up, and she pays fair and pays when the spell is done, which beats shouting at passers-by or hauling myself down to that muddy bridge half asleep. I need two pennies before dark for a proper bed, and I'd sooner earn them in the bow window beside the green velvet, where folk going by can see me.
turns.outcome: done plain sewing at Ida's window, paid 1d
turns.story:
You give the rose a pat, wave to Bet at her stall, and sweep across the cobbles to Fenn's, where the bow window is full of cloth and Ida Fenn sits sewing in the light with a mouthful of pins.

Marigold: "Mistress Fenn, goodness, your notice is still up in the square, so I've come to see if the rain's brought you fresh hems. Name me the pieces and the price first, the way we agreed, and I'll sit in your window and do them neat as you like."

Ida: "Plain hems and seams, Marigold, a penny or two a spell, if they're neat. I'll not pay for anything I've not asked for."

You take the window seat and sew. The stitches run small and even, and when the spell is done Ida turns the seam over twice and counts a penny into your hand.

turns.do: I tuck the penny away, give the rose a pat, and smile at Ida over the velvet. "Mistress Fenn, goodness, that's one penny, and a bed's two. Have you one more spell of plain hems before the lamp's lit? Name me the pieces and the price first, and I'll sew them as neat as the last."
turns.journal: Ida pays fair and pays when the spell's done, and I'm too worn out to go chasing carters' coats in the taproom. One more penny here means a proper bed tonight, and I mean to keep my place in this window until she can't do without me.
turns.outcome: refused one more spell of plain sewing at Ida's
turns.story:
You tuck your penny away, give the rose a pat, and smile at Ida over the velvet. A penny, you say, and a bed is two: is there one more spell of plain hems before the lamp is lit? You ask her to name the pieces and the price first.

Ida: *She takes a pin from her mouth and looks at you a moment over the lace collar.* "There is nothing more wanted tonight, Marigold. What you sewed is paid and settled. Come in the morning, and I'll see whether the window has hems for you."

The shop is quiet but for the tick of her needle, and the light in the bow window is going.

turns.do: I hold my penny out to Ida on my palm and give the rose a tired little pat. "Mistress Fenn, goodness, I'm worn thin as old lawn, and Tom's bed is two pennies when I've only one. Would you let me curl up on your window seat tonight for this penny? I'll not touch a thread or a bolt, and I'll be here for your hems the moment the light comes."
turns.journal: I'm too tired to sew straight for a carter, and after Abel's sneering I'd not risk another laugh in the taproom tonight. Ida has been fair to me, so I've asked her plainly and offered her my penny. Sleeping beside the green velvet and being first at her hems in the morning keeps me on my way to being the needle she can't do without.
turns.outcome: refused a night on Ida's window seat
turns.story:
You hold your penny out to Ida on your palm, give the rose a tired little pat, and ask whether you might curl up on her window seat tonight, promising not to touch a thread or a bolt and to be here for her hems the moment the light comes.

Ida takes the pins from her mouth and sets them in the cushion at her wrist, and looks you over, hem to collar.

Ida: "Keep your penny, Marigold Thimble. The window seat is for sitting and for talk, and I'm glad of both. It is not a bed, and I'll not have anyone sleeping in my shop among the cloth. Nor do I want more sewing tonight. Go and find a proper roof."

Her needle is already moving again in the lamplight. The bolts of velvet and linen sit quiet in the window, and the door to the Market Square waits behind you.

turns.do: I smooth my skirt, pin the rose its inch higher, and give Ida my brightest smile over the velvet. "Good morning, Mistress Fenn! You said to come at first light, and goodness, here I am, crumpled as yesterday's muslin but with a steady hand. Has the window any hems for me today? Name me the pieces and the price first, and I'll do them neat as the last."
turns.journal: Ida told me to come in the morning, and she pays fair and pays when the spell's done, so I'll ask her first before market day's crowd and Ned's ribbons have my penny out of my pocket. I'm working toward a loaf, a real bed tonight, and a seat in that bow window where everyone passing can see me.
turns.outcome: out_of_reach more plain sewing at Ida's window this visit
turns.story:
You smooth your skirt, pin the rose an inch higher, and give Ida Fenn your brightest smile across the velvet in the window.

Marigold Thimble: "Good morning, Mistress Fenn! You said to come at first light, and goodness, here I am, crumpled as yesterday's muslin but with a steady hand. Has the window any hems for me today? Name me the pieces and the price first, and I'll do them neat as the last."

Ida Fenn: She takes the pins from her mouth and looks you over, hem to collar, before she answers. "Marigold. There's no more plain sewing wanted at the window now. The pile is done."

The shop is quiet around you: the bolts of cloth, the brass measure on the counter's edge, Ida's needle moving again in the light. Ribbons hang in every colour in the bow window, and the door to the square stands open at your back.

turns.do: I give Ida a bright little curtsey. "Then I'll be back for the next pile, Mistress Fenn, don't you dare give it to anyone else!" I sweep down to the Wheatsheaf, rose pinned high, and call across the taproom: "Goodness, is that Master Birch's famous elbow everyone's talking about? That was my needle! A penny a tear, gentlemen, price named first and paid when you've seen it. Who's next?"
turns.journal: Ida's pile is done and a loaf would leave me nothing for a bed, so I'll go where my work is already being talked about and let Wat's coat speak for me. One more penny from a torn sleeve buys me a real night's sleep, and every coat I mend puts my name further round Wendleford.
turns.outcome: partly pennies for torn sleeves at the Wheatsheaf
turns.story:
You give Ida a bright little curtsey and promise to be back for the next pile. Out in the afternoon light of the square, Robin is standing near the pump as you cross to the Wheatsheaf, the rose pinned high in your hair.

Inside, the taproom smells of ale and woodsmoke, and Tom Harrow is behind the bar. You call across it: "Goodness, is that Master Birch's famous elbow everyone's talking about? That was my needle! A penny a tear, gentlemen, price named first and paid when you've seen it. Who's next?"

Wat Birch looks down at his sleeve and grins, tugging it out to show the room.

Wat: "Well now, friend, famous is a big word for a bit of wool, but I'll not argue. Neat work, that was, and a penny honest paid. Reckon there's no harm in you telling folk so."

He glances toward Tom and says he's after cutting work for Dunn's barley and a cheap bed, if either of them has a word on it. The carters at the tables go on with their mugs. No one else has offered you a torn sleeve yet.

turns.do: I give the rose a pat and lean on the bar with my most penitent smile. "Master Harrow, goodness, I know I made a drowned rat of your pots last time, but I've learnt my lesson. Let me have them again tonight and I'll scour every one till you can see your face in it. A supper and a few pennies if they come out right, same as before?" Then, if he nods, I roll up my sleeves and announce to the whole taproom that I'm going to show those pots what a proper finish looks like.
turns.journal: Pots are the only work here that pays a supper as well as pennies, and I'm too hollow and too tired to haggle over coats one at a time. I botched it once from hurrying, so this time I'll go slow and careful. I'm working toward a full belly and a proper bed tonight, so I'm fresh for Ida's next pile in the morning.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
You give the rose a pat and lean on the bar with your most penitent smile, and put it to Tom Harrow plainly: you made a poor job of his pots last time, you've learnt better, and you'll scour every one till he sees his face in it, for a supper and a few pennies if they come out right. Then you roll up your sleeves and tell the whole taproom you'll show those pots what a proper finish looks like.

Tom: "Go on, friend, they'll not wash themselves!" he booms, jerking his head at the door behind the bar.

The scullery is steamy and stacked high. You go slowly this time, pot by pot, scouring each with sand until the pewter shines, and when you carry the last one out Tom turns it in the firelight and grunts, satisfied. He counts three pennies into your palm and sets a bowl of stew and a heel of bread before you.

The fire crackles, the carters have started on a song, and the stew is hot.

turns.do: I put two pennies on the bar with a flourish. "Master Harrow, a bed, if you please, and goodness, I've earned it! Not a pot in the place you can't see your face in." Then I give the room a little wave, rose pinned high, and go up to sleep.
turns.journal: I've gone night after night without a proper bed and I'm frayed to the selvedge, so tonight the pennies go on sleep and not on ribbons. That still leaves me two in my pocket, and I'll be fresh and bright for Ida's window in the morning.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
You set two pennies on the bar with a flourish. "Master Harrow, a bed, if you please, and goodness, I've earned it! Not a pot in the place you can't see your face in."

Tom takes the coins into his big red hand. You give the taproom a little wave, rose pinned high, and climb the stair at the back. Below, Constance is still by the fire.

The bed takes you, and the sounds of the taproom thin and go out.

turns.do: I give the rose its inch higher, call "Good morning, Master Harrow! Good morning, Dilly, chum!" and sweep out west to the square. At Bet's stall I hold up a penny: "Goodness, Bet, tell me you've a loaf left for me before the bridge hands eat the lot!" Then I take it across to Fenn's, eating as I go.
turns.journal: Bet's loaf costs one penny where Tom's stew would cost two, so I'll still have a penny left, and Ida may have a new pile now the market's past. I'm working toward a steady seat in that bow window, two pennies by dusk for a bed, and someday a length of that green velvet for myself.
turns.outcome: done bought and ate a loaf from Bet, went to Fenn's
turns.story:
You call a bright good morning to Master Harrow and to Dilly, and sweep out of the Wheatsheaf's door into the square.

At Bet's stall you hold up your penny and ask if she has a loaf left before the bridge hands eat the lot. She has. The penny leaves your fingers and the warm loaf is yours, and you eat it as you cross the cobbles, northeast to Fenn's.

Ida Fenn sits in the bow window light with a mouthful of pins, the green velvet shining at the front of the glass. The counter stretches down the shop, quiet this morning, and the window seat is empty beside her.

turns.do: I finish the last of Bet's loaf, brush the crumbs off my skirt, and settle my most hopeful smile on Ida. "Mistress Fenn, goodness, a whole new day and the market's been and gone. Has anything come in that wants a neat hem? Name me the pieces and the price first, the way we agreed, and I'll do them right here in your window."
turns.journal: I'm already standing in her shop, so I'd be a fool not to ask before I go traipsing to the taproom, and Ida pays fair and pays when the spell's done. If she says no, the farmhands' wage-pennies are next, and either way I'm working toward a bed tonight and a steady seat beside that velvet.
turns.outcome: failed plain sewing for Ida, seams went wrong, no pay
turns.story:
You finish the last of Bet's loaf, brush the crumbs off your skirt, and turn your most hopeful smile on Ida. "Mistress Fenn, goodness, a whole new day and the market's been and gone. Has anything come in that wants a neat hem? Name me the pieces and the price first, the way we agreed, and I'll do them right here in your window."

Ida: She takes the pins from her mouth and looks you over, hem first. "Plain hemming and seaming, Marigold, a penny or two if it's neatly done. Sit."

You take a pile of linen to the window light and set to it, but the seams wander. Twice you unpick a run of stitches, and the third try is no straighter. Ida holds the work up to the light, clicks her tongue, and sets it aside to unpick herself; no coin comes across the counter.

The needle case lies open on your knee. Ida goes back to her own sewing, and the window light has begun to lengthen.

turns.do: I fold my needle case shut and give Ida a rueful little smile. "Goodness, my seams went wandering like a loose thread in a draught today. I'll come back with steadier fingers, Mistress Fenn, I promise you." Then I sweep down to the Wheatsheaf, rose pinned high, lean on the bar and say, "Master Harrow, you saw what I did with your pots last night. Same again tonight, for a supper and a few pennies if they shine?"
turns.journal: I shamed myself at Ida's window today, and pressing her now would only sour her. Tom's pots paid me three pennies and a supper the last time I took them slow and careful, and with one penny in my pocket that's my only sure road to a bed. I'm working toward a warm night's sleep and steady hands for Ida in the morning, so she'll call me neat again.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
You fold your needle case shut and give Ida a rueful little smile, and say your seams went wandering today and you'll come back with steadier fingers. Then you sweep out across the square to the Wheatsheaf, rose pinned high, and lean on the bar.

You ask Tom for the pots again, for a supper and a few pennies if they shine. Tom Harrow jerks his head at the scullery door, already reaching for the next mug.

The pots are stacked as high as ever, and this time you take them slow. The brass comes up bright, and the basin goes grey with grease before you are done. Tom looks them over, nods, and counts two pennies into your hand, with a bowl of stew and a heel of bread pushed across the bar.

Tom: "That's how it's done, Mistress Thimble!" he booms, and goes off to the taproom with a tray.

The fire is warm, and the carters have started up a song at the far end. You have three pennies in your pocket.

turns.do: I lay two pennies on the bar and give Master Harrow my brightest smile. "A bed, if you please. Two nights running, goodness, I'm practically gentry!" I give Dilly a wink and a "Better luck next time, chum," pat the rose at my collar, and climb the stair.
turns.journal: My seams wandered at Ida's today because I was frayed, and a cold night on the cobbles would only make them wander worse. A proper bed leaves me a penny in hand and fresh fingers to win back her "neat" in the morning. I'm still working toward that steady seat in her bow window, and one day a length of the green velvet.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
You lay two pennies on the bar and give Tom Harrow your brightest smile. "A bed, if you please. Two nights running, goodness, I'm practically gentry!"

Tom: "Two pennies, and welcome, friend," he booms, sweeping them into his palm without breaking stride.

You wink at Dilly, tell them, "Better luck next time, chum," pat the rose at your collar, and climb the stair. The taproom noise falls away behind you, the fire still popping at the far end, and a bed is waiting under the eaves.

turns.do: I set the rose its inch higher and call, "Good morning, Master Harrow! Good morning, Master Birch, and how's that famous elbow holding up?" Then I sweep out west to the square. "Bet, goodness, a loaf for my last penny, if you please!" I eat it on my way to Fenn's, and I ask Ida sweetly whether anything's come in that wants a neat hem, pieces and price named first.
turns.journal: I slept well, so my fingers are steady again, and Ida's window is where I'll earn a proper name and a seat beside that green velvet. Eating first means my seams won't wander. If Ida says no, the farmhands' harvest pennies are still waiting at the Wheatsheaf tonight, alongside Tom's pots.
turns.outcome: done asked Ida about hems
turns.story:
You set the rose an inch higher and call across the taproom, "Good morning, Master Harrow! Good morning, Master Birch, and how's that famous elbow holding up?"

Wat Birch: "Morning, friend!" He flexes the arm and grins tiredly. "Holds a treat, it does. Not a thread out of place since you stitched it, and a penny well spent, I reckon. You hear tell of any cutting work about, or a cheap bed? Dunn's barley wants doing, I'm told."

You sweep out through the west door into the square. At Bet Lamb's stall you ask for a loaf for your last penny, and she hands one over. You eat it as you cross the cobbles to Fenn's, and its warmth settles you.

Ida Fenn sits sewing in the bow window, pins in her mouth. "Good morning, Mistress Fenn," you say. "Has anything come in that wants a neat hem? Do tell me the pieces and the price first, and I'll not waste your thread."

Ida: She takes the pins from her mouth and looks over your hem before she answers. "A spell of plain hems and seams at the window, Marigold. A penny or two, if it's neatly done."

The needle in her hand waits for your answer.

turns.do: I give Hobb a bright little nod. "Goodness, a harness-mender! We'll make a proper sewing circle of it." Then I settle onto the window seat beside the green velvet. "Yes please, Mistress Fenn, a spell of hems and seams, a penny or two if they're neat. I'll go slow as honey this time." I take the linen into the light and make every stitch small and even, and I don't hurry a single one.
turns.journal: Ida's offer is still waiting on her needle, and if I dither that Hobb will take my whole seat in her window. I slept well and I've eaten, so my fingers are steady, and slow work won me Tom's pennies. I'm working toward a bed tonight and a name in Ida's bow window, close enough to the velvet to touch it.
turns.outcome: done hems and seams for pay
turns.story:
You give Hobb a bright little nod, say it'll be a proper sewing circle, and ask Ida for a spell of hems and seams, a penny or two if they're neat, and promise to go slow as honey this time.

You settle on the window seat beside the green velvet, take the linen into the light, and make every stitch small and even, not hurrying one. The needle goes in and out, and the seam lies straight.

Ida: She turns the hem over, draws a thumbnail along it, finds nothing to unpick, and counts two pennies into your hand.

Hobb sits near you with his own needle. The bolts of cloth glow in the afternoon, and the shop is quiet but for the thread.

turns.do: I fold my needle case shut and give Ida my brightest smile. "Two pennies and not a stitch to unpick! Goodness, Mistress Fenn, I'll be back first thing for whatever comes in." I nod to Hobb, pat the rose an inch higher at my collar, and sweep across the square to the Wheatsheaf. I lean on the bar and say, "Master Harrow, the harvest hands have left you a mountain of pots, I'll be bound. Same as last night, slow and shining, for a supper and a few pennies?"
turns.journal: The two pennies in my pocket are my bed, and Tom's pots are the only work in town that pays a supper and coin on top. If I take them slow again I'll have a full belly, a roof, and a penny or two to put towards that green velvet. Ida called my work neat today, and I mean to keep it that way.
turns.outcome: done pots for supper and pennies
turns.story:
You fold your needle case shut and tell Ida you'll be back first thing for whatever comes in. A nod to Hobb, the rose set an inch higher at your collar, and you sweep out across the square to the Wheatsheaf.

The taproom is warm with woodsmoke and stew. Leaning on the bar, you ask Tom whether the harvest hands have left him a mountain of pots, and whether it might be the same as last night, slow and shining, for a supper and a few pennies.

Tom: "Friend, they have, and I'd sooner see them in your hands than mine!" He jerks his head at the scullery door.

You take the pots one at a time and scour each until it shines. When you come out, Tom counts three pennies into your palm and sets a bowl of stew and a heel of bread before you.

Agnes sits at the end of the room. The fire crackles, and the bowl steams under your hands.

turns.do: I set two pennies on the bar. "A bed again, Master Harrow, three nights running, goodness, I'll be wanting a crest on my door!" On my way to the stair I pause by Agnes. "Mistress Pollard, if any of your bridge men tear a sleeve on those timbers, send them to me. A penny, neat as Wat Birch's elbow, and they see it before they pay." Then I pat the rose and climb up to bed.
turns.journal: Ida called my hems neat today and paid me two pennies, and I'll not throw that away with tired fingers, so the bed comes first. A word to Agnes costs nothing and might send torn coats my way. With three pennies kept back I'm one step nearer that green velvet.
turns.outcome: partly bed paid; Agnes refused the mending offer
turns.story:
You set two pennies on the bar and tell Tom he'll be wanting a crest on your door, three nights running.

Tom Harrow: "A crest and a ribbon, Marigold!" he booms, sweeping the coins into his palm.

On your way to the stair you stop by Agnes and offer your needle for any bridge man's torn sleeve: a penny, neat as Wat Birch's elbow, and they see it before they pay.

Agnes: "Marigold, isn't it? You asked me this already, and I said no. My men mend their own coats, and I've no pennies to spare on it." She taps the pencil behind her ear. "If a man wants to send himself to you on his own coin, that's his business, not mine."

You pat the rose and climb the stair to your bed. The fire crackles below, and the wind blows over the roof.

turns.do: I set the rose its inch higher and sing out, "Good morning, all! Master Hale, Master Hayle, any torn cuffs want a neat penny's mend, you know where to find me, at Fenn's window!" Then I sweep west to the square, buy a loaf from Bet for a penny, and go on to Ida and ask sweetly whether there's a spell of hems this morning, the pieces and price named first.
turns.journal: A penny loaf feeds me as well as Tom's stew for half the cost, and Ida paid me two pennies yesterday for straight seams, so her window is where I'll earn and be seen. I'm saving toward the green velvet, and every penny kept is a thread nearer it.
turns.outcome: done hems at Ida's
turns.story:
You set the rose an inch higher and sing out across the taproom, "Good morning, all! Master Hale, Master Hayle, any torn cuffs want a neat penny's mend, you know where to find me, at Fenn's window!" Then you sweep out of the Wheatsheaf's west door into the blowing, bright morning.

At the stall in the square Bet Lamb takes your penny and hands you a warm loaf, teasing you as she does. You tuck it into your bundle and go on to Fenn's bow window.

Ida Fenn looks up over her pins as you ask, sweetly, for a spell of hems, the pieces and the price named first. She sets you at the window with a pile of plain linen. Your needle runs quick and even, and the seams lie flat and true. Ida runs a thumbnail along them, nods once, and counts a penny into your palm.

The light is full in the window, and the green velvet glows beside you. Ida is already sorting the next fold of cloth.

turns.do: I break my loaf on the window seat and eat it daintily, so I get no crumbs near the velvet. "Goodness, Mistress Fenn, I'd quite forgotten my own breakfast for your linen!" Then I brush my fingers clean and say, "Is there another spell of hems wanting this afternoon? Do name the pieces and the price first, and I'll go slow as honey again."
turns.journal: My fingers are steady and Ida's thumbnail found nothing to unpick this morning, so I'll press on while she's pleased with me, but on a fed belly this time. If she says no, Tom's pots are still waiting tonight. I'm saving every penny toward that green velvet, and toward the day Ida says it suits me.
turns.outcome: refused another spell of hems this afternoon
turns.story:
You break your loaf on the window seat and eat it daintily, with a hand cupped under each bite so no crumb strays near the velvet. "Goodness, Mistress Fenn, I'd quite forgotten my own breakfast for your linen!" You brush your fingers clean. "Is there another spell of hems wanting this afternoon? Do name the pieces and the price first, and I'll go slow as honey again."

Ida: "Neatly done this morning, Marigold, I'll say that. But the hems are done for now. Come again, and we'll see what the window wants."

She takes up her needle again, a mouthful of pins, and the afternoon light slants across the green velvet in the bow window.

turns.do: I fold my needle case and give Ida my sunniest smile. "Goodnight, Mistress Fenn. I'll be back at first light with fingers as steady as this morning's." Then I sweep across the square to the Wheatsheaf, rose pinned its inch higher, lean on the bar and say, "Master Harrow, the harvest hands will have left you a fresh mountain of pots, I'll be bound. Slow and shining again, for a supper and a few pennies?"
turns.journal: Ida's hems are done for today and pressing her would only sour her, but Tom's pots have paid me every time I've gone slow. With supper and a bed paid out of the pots, my three pennies stay whole, and I'm saving them toward that green velvet and the day Ida says it suits me.
turns.outcome: done pots for supper and pennies
turns.story:
You fold your needle case, wish Mistress Fenn goodnight and promise her fingers as steady as this morning's. Then you cross the square to the Wheatsheaf, its taproom loud with carters and the smell of stew, and lean on the bar.

You tell Tom the harvest hands will have left him a fresh mountain of pots, and ask if slow and shining will earn a supper and a few pennies. Hobb is there in the taproom, near enough to hear.

Tom waves you through to the scullery, and you scour the pots one by one until they gleam. When you come out he puts two pennies in your palm and a bowl of stew in front of you. The fire cracks at the far end of the room, and the carters are starting up a song.

turns.do: I set two pennies on the bar with a flourish. "Master Harrow, a bed again, four nights running. I'll have to embroider my initials on the pillow!" On my way past the fire I tip my head to Dob Hayle. "Lovely broad lapels, Master Hayle. If they ever want a neat stitch, a penny, and you see it before you pay." Then I pat the rose and climb the stair.
turns.journal: The bed keeps my fingers steady for Ida's window, and that's where my name and my pennies are growing. A word to Dob costs nothing and might win me a coat. With three pennies kept back, I'm saving thread by thread toward that green velvet.
turns.outcome: done paid for bed, offered Dob a stitch, slept
turns.story:
You set two pennies on the bar with a flourish.

Marigold: "Master Harrow, a bed again, four nights running. I'll have to embroider my initials on the pillow!"

Tom takes the coins with a nod. On your way past the fire you tip your head to Dob Hayle.

Marigold: "Lovely broad lapels, Master Hayle. If they ever want a neat stitch, a penny, and you see it before you pay."

You pat the rose at your collar and climb the stair, and the warm noise of the taproom falls away below you. You sleep.

turns.do: I stop by Wat Birch's bench and preen a little. "Good morning, Master Birch! Is that elbow still holding? Goodness, you're my best advertisement. If any of the harvest hands tears a sleeve, do point them my way, a penny, and they see it before they pay." Then I set the rose its inch higher and sweep west to Bet's stall for a loaf. From there I go on to Fenn's, and I'll ask Ida sweetly whether there's a spell of hems this morning, pieces and price named first.
turns.journal: Wat's good word costs me nothing and might send a coat my way. Ida's window feeds my purse and lets folk see me at work, and I must be there before Hobb takes the hems. Three pennies now, and every spell of straight seams brings that green velvet a little nearer.
turns.outcome: done asked Ida for a spell of hems
turns.story:
In the taproom of the Wheatsheaf you stop by Wat Birch's bench and smile.

Marigold: "Good morning, Master Birch! Is that elbow still holding? Goodness, you're my best advertisement. If any of the harvest hands tears a sleeve, do point them my way, a penny, and they see it before they pay."

Wat Birch: "Morning to you, friend." He flexes the elbow and grins tiredly. "Reckon it's holding fine, not a thread out of place. I'll send any hand with a torn sleeve your way, a penny's fair for work like that."

You go out west into the bright, blowing square and buy a loaf from Bet for a penny. Then you cross to Fenn's, where Ida Fenn sits in the window light with pins in her mouth and the green velvet hung behind her. You ask her sweetly whether there is a spell of hems this morning, and the pieces and price named first.

Ida: "Hems and seams at the window, Marigold, and neatly. A penny or two, according to the work."

The needle case is at your side, the loaf warm in your hand, and the window seat is free.

turns.do: I sit in the window seat and eat my loaf with a hand cupped under every bite, chattering to Ida about the wind. Then I brush my fingers clean and say, "Now, Mistress Fenn, which pieces, and is it a penny or two for them? Name it, and I'll go slow as honey." Once she's named it, I thread my needle and sew small and even, right beside the velvet where the whole square can see me.
turns.journal: Ida offered the window and the seat is free, and if I dither Hobb will have the hems, so I'll take them, but fed this time and with the price settled first. Two pennies in hand and two more from this spell gets me a bed and keeps me saving toward that green velvet, and toward the day Ida says it suits me.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:

Ida: "Hems and seams, Marigold, the same as before," she says, a pin between her lips. "A penny or two for neat work. Mind the stitches."

You thread your needle and sew small and even, right beside the green velvet where anyone crossing the square can see you through the bow window. Ida watches your hem a long moment, then nods once and counts two pennies into your hand. You have four in your pocket now.

The wind rattles the window, and the afternoon light slants over the cloth.

turns.do: I fold my needle case and lay a fingertip, ever so lightly, by the green velvet. "Goodness, Mistress Fenn, I've sat beside this beauty all day and never asked. What would a length cost me, just enough for a collar and a pair of cuffs?" Once she's named it, I thank her sweetly, set the rose its inch higher, and sweep across the square to the Wheatsheaf to ask Tom for his pots, slow and shining.
turns.journal: I've been saving toward that velvet without knowing what it costs, and a seamstress who doesn't know the price of her cloth is only daydreaming. Tom's pots will pay for my bed and leave my four pennies whole, and once I know Ida's figure I'll know how many more spells of hems it will take.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
You fold your needle case and lay a fingertip, ever so lightly, by the green velvet. "Goodness, Mistress Fenn, I've sat beside this beauty all day and never asked. What would a length cost me, just enough for a collar and a pair of cuffs?"

Ida: "The velvet isn't sold by the length, Marigold," she says, a pin between her lips. "But a collar and cuffs, made up to order, four pennies." She eyes your hem, and says no more.

You thank her sweetly, set the rose its inch higher, and sweep across the square to the Wheatsheaf, where Hobb and Robin sit by the fire. "Tom, have you pots that want washing? I'll make them shine." Tom jerks his head at the scullery, and you scour the stack in the steam until they gleam. Two pennies are counted into your palm. The taproom is loud behind you.

turns.do: I set two pennies on the bar with a flourish. "Master Harrow, a bed again, five nights running! And mark me, all of you," I turn to the fire, to Hobb and Robin and Wat and Dob, "the next time I sweep through that door it'll be in Mistress Fenn's green velvet, collar and cuffs, so do look twice." Then I pat the rose and climb the stair.
turns.journal: Six pennies is a bed tonight and four left over, which is exactly what Ida asked for the velvet, so I'll pay her at first light and not risk dull fingers or a cold floor. Telling the room first means every eye will be waiting for me when I come back in green.
turns.outcome: done paid for a bed and slept
turns.story:
The fire is low and the taproom warm as you set two pennies on the bar with a flourish.

Marigold: "Master Harrow, a bed again, five nights running! And mark me, all of you," you say, turning to the fire, "the next time I sweep through that door it'll be in Mistress Fenn's green velvet, collar and cuffs, so do look twice."

Hobb and Robin are by the hearth to hear it. You pat the rose and climb the stair to your bed, and sleep comes quickly.

turns.do: I set the rose its inch higher and call to the room, "Mark the door, all of you, I'll be back in green!" Then I sweep west across the square, straight past Bet's stall, and into Fenn's. I count four pennies into Ida's palm one by one. "There, Mistress Fenn, the velvet collar and cuffs, if you please." Once they're on I turn about in the window light. "Well? Does it suit me?" Then, sweetly, "And is there a spell of hems this morning, pieces and price named first?"
turns.journal: I promised the whole taproom they'd see me in green, and four pennies is exactly the price, so the velvet comes before my breakfast. Hunger is only a morning's worth of trouble, and a spell of hems at Ida's window should buy back my loaf. What I'm working toward is walking into the Wheatsheaf tonight and having every head turn twice, and perhaps, at last, hearing Ida say it suits me.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:

You count four pennies into Ida's palm, one by one. Ida sets down her pins and hands over the green velvet collar and cuffs, and you put them on and turn about in the window light.

Marigold: "Well? Does it suit me? And is there a spell of hems this morning, pieces and price named first?"

Ida: "The velvet sits well enough, Marigold, and it's cut true; mind you keep your own hem as straight as my seams." She nods toward the window seat. "There are hems, yes. A penny or two for a neat spell, seams and all, done at the window."

The light falls green on the cuffs, and the needle waits at the window.

turns.do: I settle into the window seat with a little flourish of the cuffs so the square can see the green. "A penny or two for a neat spell, then, Mistress Fenn. I'll go slow as honey, and you'll not find a stitch to unpick." Then I thread my needle and sew small and even, keeping my hem as straight as her seams, just as she bade me.
turns.journal: Ida's hems are here and offered, and if I dither Hobb will have them. Besides, there's no better place to be seen in my new velvet than her bow window. My pockets are empty and my stomach's grumbling, so this spell must buy me a loaf, and after it Tom's pots will buy my bed. Tonight I'll walk into the Wheatsheaf in green and see who looks twice.
turns.outcome: failed sewing a neat spell for Ida
turns.story:
You settle into the window seat with a flourish of your cuffs, the green velvet catching the afternoon light for anyone crossing the square to see. "A penny or two for a neat spell, then, Mistress Fenn," you say. "I'll go slow as honey, and you'll not find a stitch to unpick."

Ida: "We shall see, Marigold," she says through her pins, and sets a heap of hems in your lap.

You thread your needle and begin, small and even. But the cloth puckers under your thumb, and the seam wanders off true. Before you have gone far Ida leans across, looks it over with her sharp eyes, and draws her pincushion hand back with a small sigh. Nothing is paid for this one.

The bow window glows, the bolts of cloth stand quiet behind the counter, and the unfinished hem lies across your knee.

turns.do: I fold the unfinished hem neatly onto Ida's counter. "Forgive me, Mistress Fenn, my fingers were all thumbs today. I'll come back fresh another morning." Then I set the rose its inch higher, smooth my velvet cuffs, and sweep across the square to the Wheatsheaf. I pause in the doorway long enough for the room to look up. "There, I promised you green!" Then I go to the bar. "Master Harrow, have you pots that want scouring? Slow and shining, I swear it."
turns.journal: Ida won't let me try the same work twice in a day, and I've not a crumb nor a penny, so Tom's pots are my only honest supper and bed, and I'll get my grand entrance in green on the way there. I'll go slow as a slipstitch and not rush, because rushed pots earn nothing, and tomorrow I'll go back to Ida's window and make my hems straight as her seams.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
At Fenn's you fold the unfinished hem onto Ida's counter and say your fingers were all thumbs today and you will come back fresh another morning. Then you set the ribbon its inch higher, smooth the green velvet cuffs, and sweep across the square to the Wheatsheaf.

You pause in the doorway until the room looks up, and call out that you promised them green. At the bar you ask Tom Harrow if he has pots that want scouring, slow and shining.

Tom: "Pots, is it? Through the back, Marigold."

You go through to the steamy scullery and work through the stack, slowly, until each one shines. Tom gives you your supper for it, stew and a heel of bread eaten at the end of the bar, and two pennies in your hand. The taproom's fire crackles; the stair at the back leads up to the beds.

turns.do: I lay my two pennies on the bar and give my velvet cuffs a little flourish as I do it. "Master Harrow, a bed, six nights running now! Robin, Mistress Pollard, do look, didn't I promise you green?" I wait just long enough for somebody to say something kind, then smooth the rose and climb the stair.
turns.journal: My fingers went all thumbs today, so a good night's sleep comes before anything else if my hems are to run straight as Ida's seams tomorrow. Two pennies is exactly a bed. I'm working toward Ida paying me fair again, and toward a room that turns its head when I come in wearing green.
turns.outcome: done
turns.story:
You lay your two pennies on the bar and give your velvet cuffs a little flourish as you do it. The fire has burned low, and Tom Harrow takes the coins with a nod.

Marigold: "Master Harrow, a bed, six nights running now! Robin, Mistress Pollard, do look, didn't I promise you green?"

Robin is curled asleep where they lie and does not stir. You smooth the rose at your collar and climb the stair to your bed, and sleep comes over you.

turns.do: I give the room a flourish of my cuffs on the way out. "Good morning, Robin, Dilly! Green, as I promised!" Then I sweep west past Bet's stall and into Fenn's. "Mistress Fenn, I've slept and my fingers are my own again. Is there a spell of hems this morning? Name the pieces and the price, and I'll sew them small and slow, straight as your own seams."
turns.journal: My pockets are empty and my stomach's hollow, and Ida's morning hems are the surest penny in Wendleford, so I must be at her window before Hobb is. Yesterday's wandering seam still stings, and I mean to have her run her thumbnail along today's and find nothing to unpick. Then a loaf, Tom's pots tonight, and the velvet glowing in her window all day for the square to see.
turns.outcome: failed a spell of hems at Ida's window
turns.story:
You give your cuffs a flourish on the way out of the Wheatsheaf. "Good morning, Robin, Dilly! Green, as I promised!" Then you cross the damp cobbles of the Market Square, past Bet's striped awning, and push into Fenn's.

Ida Fenn sits in the bow window with pins in her mouth and a hem across her knee. You tell her you've slept and your fingers are your own again, and ask for a spell of hems, the pieces and the price named, sewn small and slow and straight as her own seams.

You take up the needle at the window seat. The light is good and the cloth is plain, but the stitches wander under your fingers, one drifting off its line, then the next, and the hem puckers where it should lie flat. Ida takes it from you, runs a thumbnail along it, and sets it aside without a word. No pennies come across the counter.

The window glows with the length of green velvet, and the shop is quiet but for the snip of her scissors. Ida is waiting to see what you do next.

turns.do: I fold my hands over my cuffs and give Ida a rueful little smile. "Not my day for your hems, Mistress Fenn, but I'll be back fresh another morning, you'll see." Then I nod to Hobb, sweetly, and sweep out across the square to the Wheatsheaf. "Master Harrow, any pots wanting scouring? I'll go slow as a slipstitch, every one shining."
turns.journal: My seams wandered twice now, and Ida won't have me at them again today, while Hobb sits there stitching neatly in my place. That stings, so I'll be at Tom's pots before Hobb can be. Slow pots mean supper and a bed, and I can face that window again tomorrow with my green velvet and a steady hand.
turns.outcome: failed scour pots
turns.story:

You say: "Master Harrow, any pots wanting scouring? I'll go slow as a slipstitch, every one shining."

Tom: "Marigold, friend, there's always pots!" he booms over a tray of mugs, and jerks his chin toward the scullery door.

You roll your sleeves above the velvet cuffs and set to the pots in the steam. The grease will not shift; the pans slip in your hands and come out streaked, and Tom takes one look, shakes his head, and puts them back in the pile. Nothing is paid.

The taproom hums behind you, and the pile of dirty pots has hardly grown smaller.

turns.do: I flourish my cuffs and settle beside Robin with my needle case open. "Robin, goodness, that cuff of yours is fraying like a moth's breakfast still. One penny, paid after, and I'll close it neat as Wat's elbow, which still holds, ask him. Right here by the fire, so you can watch every stitch."
turns.journal: Tom won't have me back at his pots tonight, and Robin's cuff is the only bit of mending I know of under this roof, so I've named my price first, as I promised myself I would. One penny won't buy a bed, but it's a loaf in the morning and a start, and a neat mend done in front of the whole room is the best advertisement I've got.
turns.outcome: done offered the cuff mend
turns.story:

Hobb and Hester sit nearby in the taproom, and the carters go on with their talk of the flood. Robin's cuff hangs frayed at the wrist, and your offer is out in the warm air between you.

turns.do: I hold the needle case open on my knee and give Robin my brightest smile. "Go on, Robin. One penny, and only when you're pleased with it. You'll be the best-cuffed man on the whole bridge." If Robin nods, I thread up and sew slow as honey, small and even, and I hold the wrist up to the firelight so the room can see.
turns.journal: My offer is already out, and pushing on to someone else before Robin's answered would only look grasping. A slow, neat mend done in front of Hobb, Hester and the reeve would win back a bit of the pride my wandering seams cost me, and a penny is a loaf. I mean to have steady hands again, and my velvet noticed for good work as well as good looks.
turns.outcome: done offered Robin the cuff mend
turns.story:

Marigold: "Go on, Robin. One penny, and only when you're pleased with it. You'll be the best-cuffed man on the whole bridge."

The needle waits in your fingers, the thread ready, while the firelight catches the fraying edge of Robin's cuff.

turns.do: I give my cuffs a little flourish at the bar. "Good morning, Master Harrow! It's a new day, so do let me at your breakfast pots. I'll go slow as a slipstitch and not rush a single one, I swear it on my velvet." Then I roll my sleeves up above the green and take each pot as it comes, sanding it till it shines before I so much as glance at the next.
turns.journal: My fingers have wandered at Ida's twice now, and I'm hollow and half-asleep, so I'd only botch her hems again; Tom's pots will put stew in me and pennies in my pocket first. Fed and with a bed bought, I'll go back to Ida's window steady-handed and have her say "neatly done" again, and one day "it suits you."
turns.outcome: out_of_reach scullery pots, already worked this visit

Tom: "Morning to you, friend!" He swings the cloth off his shoulder and looks through the scullery door at the pots, then shakes his head. "There's nothing left in there for you just now. Come back to me later, and we'll see."

You roll your sleeves up above the green all the same, and the fire crackles at the far end of the taproom. Dilly and Hester are near, and Tom has already turned to the next mug.

turns.do: I give Wat a little wave of my velvet cuff as I pass. "Afternoon, Wat! Is that elbow still holding?" Then I lean on the bar. "Master Harrow, you said come back later, and here I am, later as you like. Let me at the pots, and I'll take every one slow as honey and sand it till it shines before I touch the next."
turns.journal: Tom told me himself to come back, and I've gone a whole day without a crumb, so his pots are the surest supper and bed in Wendleford. I mustn't rush them this time, pot by pot. Fed and rested, I'll have steady fingers for Ida's hems tomorrow and keep my green velvet looking grand.
turns.outcome: refused pots work at the Wheatsheaf, nothing more this visit
turns.story:

Wat Birch: "Afternoon, Marigold!" He tugs at his sleeve and grins. "Holding fine, friend, not a thread out of place. Best penny I ever spent."

You lean on the bar. "Master Harrow, you said come back later, and here I am, later as you like. Let me at the pots, and I'll take every one slow as honey and sand it till it shines before I touch the next."

Tom: "Ah, Marigold," says Tom, wiping his hands on the cloth over his shoulder, "the scullery's nothing more for you this visit, friend. Steam's all that's left in there." Behind him the pots stand scoured and stacked, and the fire crackles at the far end of the taproom.

turns.do: I smooth my velvet cuffs and cross to the reeve's table with my brightest smile. "Mistress Pollard, they say you're wanting hands for the bridge. I'll not wade a step, mind, but I've the neatest fingers in Wendleford for lashing, binding or stitching, if it's done from the dry bank. Name me the work and the price first, and I'll do it slow and true, as Wat's elbow can tell you."
turns.journal: Tom's scullery is done for today, and Ida's hems have gone wrong on me twice, so the reeve asking for hands is the only fresh door left open tonight. She snubbed me once and I've not forgotten, but a penny's a penny, and I'll be working on dry ground. I want a full stomach and a bed, and my velvet seen at the bridge, where everyone's looking.
turns.outcome: refused dry-bank work at a named price
turns.story:
You smooth your velvet cuffs and cross the taproom to the reeve's table, smiling your brightest, and say your piece: the neat fingers, the dry bank, the price named first.

Agnes: "Well, then, Marigold," she says, not looking up from her pencil. "I've no job called dry bank only, and I'll not name a price I can't promise. The tin's nearly empty. The work is on the bridge, and whoever puts their back into it is paid in hand when the spell's done, same as the rest. Lend your fingers there, and you're paid like them. If not, we've nothing more to say on it."

The fire pops at the far end of the room. Tom's stew steams behind the bar, and the reeve waits, pencil poised, for your answer.

turns.do: I smooth my cuffs and give Agnes a bright little nod. "Very well, Mistress Pollard, put me down. I'll be at the bridge at first light and lend my fingers wherever you put me, the same as the rest, and paid in hand when the spell's done. I'll lash and bind as neat as any hem, and I'll keep well clear of the deep water, mind." Then I wait to see her write my name.
turns.journal: Tom's scullery is spent and Ida's hems have gone wrong on me, so the bridge is the only door left with a penny behind it, and Agnes has named fair terms even if she named them coolly. I'd sooner be paid like the rest than not at all. I mean to come home from that bank with pennies for bread and a bed, and with Wendleford having seen green velvet doing honest work.
turns.outcome: done

Agnes: "I keep no list, Marigold. Come at first light, work the spell, and you're paid in hand when it's done, same as anyone. Jory Crane will put you where you're wanted. Mind the wet timber, and mind what he tells you."

No name is written. The fire ticks low beside you, and Tom clatters about behind the bar.

turns.do: I tug my velvet cuffs straight and sing out across the taproom, "Robin, I'm off to the bridge like a proper hand, so don't say Marigold Thimble never kept her word!" Then I sweep out west through the square and down the south road to the bridge. I'll find Jory Crane there and ask him, bright as a new pin, where he wants my fingers, lashing or binding, on the dry side of the wet timber.
turns.journal: I told Agnes first light, and the bridge is the only work in town that's promised to pay whoever turns up, while Tom's scullery and Ida's window keep turning me away. I'm faint with hunger and I can't face another day of noes. A spell at the bridge means bread and a bed, and the whole of Wendleford seeing green velvet do honest work.
turns.outcome: partly reached the bridge; Jory not there, bridge work over
turns.story:
You tug your velvet cuffs straight and sing out across the taproom to Robin that you are off to the bridge like a proper hand, so no one can say Marigold Thimble never kept her word. Then you sweep out by the west door, across the Market Square and down the south road to the river.

The new bridge stands whole between the two stone piers, a span of fresh yellow timber with a rail on either side, and the frame that was going up is gone. There is no one hauling or lashing on it. Agnes is on the bank; Jory Crane is nowhere about.

Your purse is empty, and the water runs quietly under the new planks.

turns.do: I put a hand to my velvet collar and give Agnes a rueful little smile. "Goodness, Mistress Pollard, I came for work and found it all finished, bright as a new pin. I'm dropping like a loose hem, so might I have the hayloft beside Robin tonight? No light, I promise, and I'll leave not a stalk out of place." Then I'll go up to the Wheatsheaf and stand first in line for Tom's pots.
turns.journal: The bridge doesn't need me after all, but a free roof costs nothing to ask for, and I can't sew straight or scour clean on no sleep at all. Once I've slept I'll have the steady fingers that win back Ida's "neatly done," and the pennies that keep my velvet out of the mud.
turns.outcome: partly hayloft leave granted; pots failed

Agnes: "Well, then. The hayloft is anyone's with my leave, and you have it, Mistress...Thimble, is it? Make your bed beside Robin if you like. No light up there, mind, not a candle, not a spark. And you'll find no work on the bridge now, it's finished."

You climb the road to the Market Square and cross it to the Wheatsheaf, where the taproom smells of ale and woodsmoke. You go through to the scullery and take up the first of Tom's pots, but the grease will not come away and the work goes wrong under your hands. Nothing is paid, and the pots are left as they were.

turns.do: I smooth my cuffs and stop by the reeve's table. "Mistress Pollard, which way's the tithe barn? I'm taking you at your word about that hayloft, no candle, not a spark." Then I give Wat a little wave of green velvet, "Goodnight, Wat, and send me those torn sleeves!", and go out west to find my bed of hay.
turns.journal: Tom won't let me at the pots again tonight, and nobody stands a stew for a girl just because her collar's pretty. A free roof is the one thing I can have, and I've botched everything lately because I'm dropping on my feet. I mean to be first in Ida's bow window in the morning, rested, sewing slow as honey, and earn my loaf and her "neatly done" back.
turns.outcome: done asked the way, went to the hayloft and slept
turns.story:

Agnes: "The hayloft's yours for the night, as I said. Tom there will point you to the tithe barn, it's no secret. No light up there, mind."

You give Wat a little wave of green velvet and bid him goodnight, and call after him to send you his torn sleeves. Then you go out west into the evening, across the cobbles of the square and in at the great doors of the tithe barn, where the floor lies empty and swept and someone in a brown coat is already inside. You climb the ladder to the hay and lie down in it, and sleep takes you quickly.

Name me the pieces and the price first, and I'll sew them slow as honey and straight as a ruled line."

turns.outcome: done asked Ida for a spell of hems and the price
turns.story:
In the tithe barn you brush the hay from your velvet and pin the rose ribbon an inch higher at the collar. Then you hurry out through the great doors and across the square, still damp in its low corners, and in at Fenn's door.

Ida Fenn sits sewing in the bow window with a mouthful of pins. Robin is there too.

Marigold: "Good morning, Mistress Fenn! I've slept, I'm steady as a plumb line, and I'd dearly love a spell of plain hems at your window. Name me the pieces and the price first, and I'll sew them slow as honey and straight as a ruled line."

Ida: She takes the pins from her mouth and looks you over, collar to hem. "Good morning, Marigold. Plain hemming and seaming at the window is a penny or two a spell, as ever, and neatly done or not at all."

The window seat is free, and the needle is in her hand.

turns.do: I settle into the free window seat beside the green velvet and smooth my cuffs. "Then put me down for a spell, Mistress Fenn. Show me exactly which pieces, and is it one penny or two for the lot? Once we've agreed, I'll go slow as honey and you'll find nothing to unpick." Then I wait for her to hand them over before I thread a single needle.
turns.journal: Ida's needle is out and her seat is free right now, and her terms are already said aloud, so this is the surest penny within reach. I've slept a little at last. I'll settle the pieces first and sew slow, then hurry to Tom's pots before the others get there, so I can buy bread, a bed, and Ida's good word.
turns.outcome: done sewed a spell for Ida

Ida Fenn sets her pins aside, hands you the work, and watches your first stitches with her sharp eyes. The light falls warm across the seam. You go slowly, and the hem comes out even, with nothing she'd care to unpick.

Ida Fenn: "Neat," she says, turning the edge over in her fingers. "A penny, and well earned." The coin is pressed into your palm.

Robin Hale is in the shop with you, and the afternoon is still bright beyond the bow window.

turns.do: I tuck the penny into my cuff and give Ida my brightest smile. "Thank you, Mistress Fenn, and I'll be back in the morning, steady as a plumb line." Then I hurry out southwest across the square to Bet's stall. "Bet, dear, have you a warm loaf left? Here's my penny, and goodness, I've never been so glad to spend one."
turns.journal: I've gone days without eating, and the last time I scoured Tom's pots hungry I made a mess of them, so bread comes before any more work. Once I've eaten I'll sleep in the hayloft for nothing and be at Ida's window first thing tomorrow, sewing slow and true, putting pennies back toward a bed and some fine things.
turns.outcome: done

The square is quiet. The tithe barn's great doors loom on the north side, and Dob Hayle, the carter, sits nearby.

I give Dob a little wave as I pass, then cross north to the tithe barn, climb up into the hay, no candle and not a spark, and curl up to sleep.

Robin is already in the window light, and Ida makes room for you at the seam. You sew slowly, a stitch at a time, and when you're done Ida turns the hem over, nods, and counts two pennies into your hand.

The pins are bright in the window, and the day is only just begun.

turns.do: I tuck my two pennies into my cuff and give Ida a little curtsey. "Two pennies, Mistress Fenn, and not a stitch unpicked! You might say it suits me, the honest work, I mean." Then I sweep out southwest to Bet's stall. "Bet, dear, a warm loaf, please. Here's a penny, and I'm keeping its brother for luck."

turns.outcome: done

Bet: "There you are, love," she says with a laugh, and hands over a loaf still warm through its cloth.

One penny left in your cuff, and the loaf in your hands.

Once I've eaten the last crumb, I brush off my velvet cuffs, tuck my penny safe in my cuff, and cross north to the tithe barn. I climb into the hay with no candle and not a spark, and sleep.

Then you cross the dim square and go north through the great doors of the tithe barn. Hester and Robin lie sleeping inside, still as stones. You climb the ladder with no candle and not a spark, ease down into the soft dusty hay, and sleep.

Bet: "Ha! Luckier than my bread? Not in this square, love," she says, and tucks a loaf into your hands, warm through the cloth.

The wind tugs at your ribbon, and the loaf steams in your hands.

While I eat I'll fish for a kind word and maybe a mending job from Dob, then rest in the hay and be first at Ida's window in the morning, saving penny by penny toward a bed and a ribbon of my own.

Bet: "Eat, love," she says, and her laugh carries across the cobbles.

Dob: "Aye, the green's well enough on you, mind. Can't say I've thought much on it." He glances down at his lapels. "The coat's served me on the road, and I'll not say it's the lapels I'm worried about. Folk who stitch for a penny want watching, I've found."

Hester stands a few paces off, looking over the stall. The wind snaps the awning, and the crust is still warm in your hand.

I pat my cuffs, wish Bet and Hester a bright goodnight, and cross north to the tithe barn. Then I climb into the hay, no candle and not a spark, and sleep.

turns.outcome: done
turns.story:

Inside, the great floor is swept and empty, the reeve's table and stool standing by the door. Robin Hale is there, a lean figure in a travel-worn brown coat. You climb the ladder to the hayloft, light no candle and strike no spark, and settle into the dusty hay. Sleep comes.
