interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question to bring a girl before she's had her breakfast! I'm hungry, I'm stiff from the hay, and I'm wearing the finest green velvet collar in Wendleford, so I should think I'm person enough. Though you might say it suits me, since you're standing there looking at it.
lines.thought: That's Robin's sort of question, and it snags on the same loose thread as the cuff that feels new every time I offer to mend it. I'll worry at it later, once I've a loaf in me and a penny back in my cuff.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: Goodness, made? Well, so's a good coat, and nobody tells the man wearing it that he's only pretending to be warm. If Wendleford's a made thing, someone cut it true: Bet's loaves are hot, Ida's thumbnail is sharp, and my stomach's as empty as any real one ever was. Now, if you're the one who stitched it all, you might have put a ribbon stall nearer the barn.
lines.thought: That's the same sort of question Robin keeps asking, about lost mornings and seams I don't remember sewing, and I don't like how it snags. I'll laugh it off for now and go get a loaf, but I'm going to ask Robin what they've written about me in that notebook.

sc.trait: I say aloud everything I'm doing, and I like an audience for it

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Goodness, proof's a tall order before breakfast. I suppose if I found a seam I'd sworn I sewed and it was never there, or if Robin's little notebook said I'd offered to mend that cuff a dozen times and each time felt like the first, well, that might give me a pucker of doubt. But a made thing that feels hunger and stings when it's ignored is near enough real for me, so unless you've a warm loaf to settle it, I'll go on believing my own stomach.
lines.thought: That's the second odd question about seams and things that come round new, and Robin's is still caught in me like a loose thread. I'll think on it properly once I've eaten, and I'll not tell this stranger they've rattled me.

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Goodness, no, I don't see how it could. Tomorrow I'll still want a loaf, I'll still be first and slowest at Ida's window, and I'll still be saving toward a ribbon, because a made penny buys a made loaf just the same. Though if you're the stitcher, I'd thank you kindly for a morning where my seams run true, and perhaps for someone to tell me the green suits me.
lines.thought: It's a brave answer, but Robin's notebook and that cuff do tug at me like a dropped stitch. I'll not let a stranger see it, though. I'll ask Robin quietly to show me what's written there.

sc.trait: I want a few fine things of my own, even if it's only a ribbon

lines.question: You said finding a seam you'd sworn you sewed, and it was never there, might give you a pucker of doubt; if that happened, whose word would you want on whether the seam was ever there?
because: Evidence = shared, corroborated.
Marigold and Robin interlock over the cuff and his questions.

lines.line: You said finding a seam you'd sworn you sewed, and it was never there, might give you a pucker of doubt; if that happened, whose word would you want on whether the seam was ever there?
lines.say: Goodness, Ida's, of course. She runs that thumbnail down every seam that crosses her counter, and she remembers a pucker longer than I remember a compliment. And Robin's little notebook, I suppose, since Robin writes everything down. But if the two of them swore the seam was never there and my fingers still remembered sewing it, well, I'd want to see the cloth itself, because cloth doesn't flatter and it doesn't lie.
lines.thought: It's odd that I'd trust Ida's thumbnail and Robin's pencil sooner than my own memory, and odder still that it doesn't frighten me as much as it ought to. All the same, that's two people now asking about seams I don't remember, and I mean to find out what Robin's been writing about me.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question to bring to a barn door before breakfast! I'm hungry, I'm stiff from the hay, and I've a rose ribbon pinned an inch higher than yesterday, so I'd say that's person enough for anyone. Though you're the second soul this week to ask me something peculiar about myself. Is it going round, like the gleaners' gossip?
lines.thought: First Robin and the cuff that always feels new, now a stranger asking whether I'm truly a person. It nags like a loose thread I can't find the end of, and I'd sooner be told my collar's lovely than be asked what I'm made of.

sc.trait: I say aloud everything I'm doing, and I like an audience for it

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: Made? Well, everything worth looking at is made, love. My collar's made, Ida's window's made, and that new bridge was nothing but a heap of yellow timber a week ago. If somebody stitched this whole town together, I'd only want to know who did the seams, because Dob Hayle's lapels could do with a word. Now, have you got a kind thing to say about my velvet, or did you only come to rattle me before my loaf?
lines.thought: That's two people now asking whether things are real or remembered, and Robin with that little notebook full of lost mornings. It sits on me like a hem I can't recall sewing. Still, bread first and the window second, and I'll worry at the loose thread when my hands are steady.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? Goodness, I'd want to turn it inside out and look at the back, the way I do with any seam. A real thing shows its knots and its puckers underneath, and I've plenty of those, empty pockets and a crooked hem only yesterday. If I ever found a seam I swore I'd never sewn, well, then I might start to wonder. Now walk me to Bet's stall and ask me over a loaf, there's a dear. I haven't a penny, but I'll talk you round to it.
lines.thought: Robin asked whether my offers feel new each time, and they do, and that sits under my collar like a pin I can't find. I'll not let a stranger see it worries me, though. I'd sooner they noticed the velvet.

sc.trait: I'd sooner talk someone round

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Tomorrow? Goodness, no. Tomorrow I'll still want my loaf, I'll still want Ida's window before Hobb gets it, and I'll still sew slow as treacle for my two pennies, made thing or not. A hem's either straight or it isn't, love, and nobody pays for wondering. Though if I'm stitched together, I'd like it known I was stitched in green velvet.
lines.thought: Robin's notebook, now this stranger, all of them asking whether things feel new to me, and I can't shake that it did feel new each time I offered to mend that cuff. I'll not let it fray me, though. I'll tuck it away like a loose thread to snip later, and get myself fed and first to the window.

sc.trait: I want a few fine things of my own

lines.question: You said you might start to wonder if you found a seam you swore you'd never sewn; how would you tell a seam you never sewed from one you've simply forgotten sewing?
because: Doubt only if a seam she swore she sewed was never there, or Robin's notebook showed a dozen cuff offers each feeling first.
Marigold's and Dilly's tests point at their own Set 3 gaps, unjoined;

lines.line: You said you might start to wonder if you found a seam you swore you'd never sewn; how would you tell a seam you never sewed from one you've simply forgotten sewing?
lines.say: Goodness, that's easy, love: by the hand. Every stitcher's got her own little habits, how tight she pulls, how long she makes the stitch, which way the knot sits, and I'd know mine across a room like I'd know my own face in Ida's glass. A seam I'd only forgotten would still be in my hand, so it's only a seam in a stranger's hand, sitting in my own work, that would give me a turn. Now, Bet's stall, and you can tell me whether the rose sits better an inch higher.
lines.thought: That's twice now, Robin's cuff and this stranger, and both times it comes round to things I don't remember doing. I'll look at the back of that cuff next time Robin holds it out, and see whose stitches are already there.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: Goodness, at this hour, with hay still in my hair? No, I can't say He's ever spoken to me, not in words. Constance Lowe's the one for that, and she's just there, she'll tell you how He showed her the hook's reach. If He ever does speak to me, I hope He mentions this collar, because it's cut true and nobody else in Wendleford will say so.
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door with a question like that, and I didn't even get a look at their coat first. I'm hollow, I haven't a penny, and I'll need a word with Bet about bread before Ida's window or I'll pucker another hem.

sc.trait: I want to be looked at twice when I walk into a room

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question to put to a girl who hasn't had her breakfast! I suppose I know a thing's meant for me when somebody looks twice at it, or at me doing it. When my needle's going slow and true and Ida runs her thumbnail down the seam and finds nothing to unpick, that feels like it was meant. Puckers never feel meant, I'll tell you that for nothing.
lines.thought: That's a prettier answer than the truth. Mostly I do whatever gets me a penny and a kind word, and I'm not sure I'd know "meant" if it walked in wearing velvet. And I'm hollow again with no penny for Bet, so whatever's meant for me this morning had better pay.

sc.trait: I want to be looked at twice when I walk into a room

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: Goodness, I'd say they're very likely right, and I'd thank them for the compliment! My own thoughts are the only ones I've got, and I've had to sew a good many of them straight before they'd lie flat. I never said Heaven pins my hems for me. It's me and my needle, slow and true, and a pair of eyes that look twice.
lines.thought: Still, it's a funny thing how Robin's question keeps tugging at me, about offers that feel new every time. Whose thoughts are those, if they don't remember being thought before?

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Goodness, what a nasty little question to bring to a barn door! I saw Agnes run her thumb over the lock and call it her box, and that's all I know. I never saw the inside of it, and I shan't go guessing at what's in other people's boxes. Constance hooked it out of the brown fair and square, and she's been nothing but kind, so if you've a worry about the wages, take it to Agnes at her table and not to a girl in a hayloft.
lines.thought: Agnes did say "not light enough yet" last night, and that's been snagging at me like a burr in wool. But I'll not hang a doubt on Constance for a stranger who asks about God and missing wages in the same breath. I'll keep my ears open, though.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.question: You said a thing feels meant when somebody looks twice at it; if you sewed a seam slow and true and nobody ever looked at it, would it still have been meant?
because: Marigold wants to be looked at twice.
Trust keyed to dignity in company.

lines.line: You said a thing feels meant when somebody looks twice at it; if you sewed a seam slow and true and nobody ever looked at it, would it still have been meant?
lines.say: Goodness, you do know where to put a pin, don't you? I'd like to say yes, that a true seam's true whether or not anyone runs a thumbnail down it, and I suppose it is, since the cloth holds just the same. But I'll be honest with you: I'd sew it slower and gladder with somebody watching, and I'd much rather they did.
lines.thought: That one pricked, because half my seams are hidden inside hems and nobody ever looks twice at those. And I'm standing here unfed and frayed, which is exactly how my stitches go crooked, so I'd better find bread before I go philosophising myself into another puckered morning.

sc.trait: I like an audience for it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: Goodness, at this hour, with hay still in my velvet? God's never said a word to me, not like He does to Constance, who'll tell you He showed her the very spot for Agnes's box. If He did speak, I fancy He'd sound like good silk being cut. I'd much sooner He sent me a warm loaf and a kind word about my collar. Do you like it? Ida Fenn made it up for me.
lines.thought: That's a peculiar question to bring to a barn door, nearly as odd as Robin's about the cuff, and it's left me feeling a bit unpicked. Still, a stranger who wants to talk is an audience, and I'd give a great deal for someone to notice the green before I go and beg my breakfast.

sc.trait: I want to be looked at twice when I walk into a room

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question for an empty stomach! I suppose I know a thing's meant for me when my hands go slow and true, and somebody looks twice and says "neat." When I'm hollow and frayed my seams wander off like they've somewhere better to be, and I take that as a sign it wasn't meant just then. Mind, you never did say about my collar.
lines.thought: Two strangers' questions before breakfast, and both of them about meaning and being given things, much like Robin's notebook ones. I've not a penny for Bet's loaf this morning, so I'd best find out what's meant for me quickly, before Hobb gets to Ida's window.

sc.trait: I want to be looked at twice when I walk into a room

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: Only my own thoughts? Goodness, I'd say they're the only ones I've got, and I've had to be quite clever with them, thank you very much! Whether it's God or my own good sense that tells me to eat before I sew, my hems come out straighter for it, so I shan't quarrel over whose voice it is. You've asked me three deep questions now and still not a word about my collar. Ida cut it true, you know.
lines.thought: Robin with the cuff, now this stranger asking whose thoughts I'm thinking. It's like someone's tugging at a seam I can't see, and I don't care for it. I'm still hollow and tired, though, so the loaf and Ida's window come first and the puzzling can wait.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Goodness, gone from it? I never heard that. I only saw Agnes run her thumb over the lock and say it was her box, and she counted Constance six pennies, kind as you like. The river's a greedy old thing, and if it got the lid up it might have had the lot, but I'll not hear a word against Constance, who's blessed me over Bet's bread more than once. Still, Agnes did say last night she wasn't "light enough yet," which is a funny way to put it, isn't it? And you *still* haven't said a word about my collar.
lines.thought: Not light enough yet. I took it for weariness, but it's snagging now like a burr in wool. I'll keep my eyes open, and my mouth shut about it till I know more.

sc.bp: Constance blessed her over Bet's bread more than once; claims to have seen Agnes check the box and count the pennies
sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.question: You said that when you're hollow and frayed your seams wander and you take that as a sign it wasn't meant just then; how do you tell a sign from simply being hungry?
because: Meant = when somebody looks twice.

lines.line: You said that when you're hollow and frayed your seams wander and you take that as a sign it wasn't meant just then; how do you tell a sign from simply being hungry?
lines.say: Goodness, you've caught me out there, haven't you? I suppose I can't tell them apart, not really. Hungry is hungry, and a sign is only a grand name I give it so I needn't feel such a fool for botching Ida's hem. So I'll call it plain sense and eat first, and right now my stomach's making more noise than any angel. Have you a penny for a mended cuff, by any chance? And it's a *lovely* collar, you know, if you'd only look.
lines.thought: They've a way of picking at a thread until the whole hem comes loose, and I don't much care for how near the bone that one went. I've no penny and no loaf, and that's no sign of anything except that I'd best be first at Ida's window.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: Goodness, God? Not to me, love, or if He does He's got a voice like wet flannel and I've never caught a word. Constance Lowe's the one He talks to, she'll tell you how He showed her the wage box in the river. Mostly what speaks to me is a good bit of velvet in a draper's window, and it's speaking now. Do you like my collar?
lines.thought: That's a peculiar thing to come asking a stranger at first light, nearly as odd as Robin's notebook questions, and I'd like to know who sent them my way. My stomach's hollow and I haven't a penny, so I mustn't stand chattering long before Ida's window fills up.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question for this early, and me not even breakfasted! I suppose I know a thing's meant for me when it shines a bit. A ribbon in a window, a seat by the light, somebody saying "neat" and meaning it. And mostly, love, when someone pays me first and tells me plainly what they want, because I've learned the hard way what comes of sewing a whole night on a guess.
lines.thought: They've asked about God and now about what's meant for me, the way Robin goes about with that little notebook. It makes me wonder whether there's a whole set of these odd questioners in Wendleford. I'm hollow and tired again with not a penny in my cuff, so whatever's meant for me today had better start with Bet's loaf, and I mustn't sit down to Ida's hems until I've had it.

sc.trait: I want a few fine things of my own, even if it's only a ribbon

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: Goodness, I'd say they're very likely right, and what of it? My own thoughts are the only ones I've got to dress up in, and they've done me well enough. Though if a thought tells me to be first at Ida's window rested and slow, I'll follow it whether it came from heaven or from my own stomach. Now, you never did say about my collar.
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no compliments, like Robin with a notebook. But that loose thread nags: those offers to Robin did feel new each time, and I'd like to know whose thoughts those were.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Goodness, wages gone? Well, I'd say the river's a greedy old thing and it can pick a lock as well as any thief, love. Though Mistress Pollard did tell me last night she's "not light enough yet," and I did wonder what she meant. But I won't hear a word against Constance, she's been kinder to me than half this parish. And you still haven't said a thing about my collar!
lines.thought: That's the second odd question about that box, and nobody asks a thing like that for no reason. I'll keep Agnes's "not light enough" folded away like a scrap that might match something later. And this one's no more noticed my velvet than Dob did.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.question: You said a thing is meant for you when it shines a bit, so has something ever shone for you and then turned out to be a mistake?
because: Concedes sign = hunger/shame cover; deflects with charm.
Marigold r3: Agnes's "light enough yet"; whether she still reaches for "sign" after conceding hunger.

lines.line: You said a thing is meant for you when it shines a bit, so has something ever shone for you and then turned out to be a mistake?
lines.say: Goodness, more times than I've had hot dinners, love! Ida's lamp shone on that window seat one night and I sewed till dawn thinking I was wanted, and come morning it was "I never asked for the rest," and not a penny for it. And yesterday the light shone on my seam, I was too hollow to see it straight, and it puckered like a drawstring bag. So now I let a thing shine and then ask what it costs before I touch a needle to it. That's sense, isn't it? Say it's sense.
lines.thought: That whole night still smarts, and so does yesterday's crooked hem, and this stranger keeps tugging at threads I'd sooner leave tucked in. I'm hungry, not a penny on me, and still not one word about my collar.

sc.trait: I say aloud everything I'm doing, and I like an audience for it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question to bring to a barn door before breakfast! Ten pennies? I'd hold them up in the middle of the square and sing out for whoever dropped them. Somebody in this town is counting every penny, and I've been that somebody, haven't I? And if nobody claimed them by nightfall, well, I'd have the rose ribbon and the blue one too, and I'd wear them both so the whole square knew where their luck had gone.
lines.thought: Ten pennies would be a bed, a loaf and Ida's whole window, and my stomach's hollow enough to tell me so. But I know what it is to lose a penny in this town, and I'd sooner have folk look twice at me for being honest than look away.

sc.trait: Pennies burn in my pocket, and a ribbon will have them out of it

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Goodness, you do go straight for the seams, don't you? For a friend who'd been good to me, oh, I'd tell a little white one, the sort you'd stitch over a tear so nobody sees the patch. I'd say Bet's loaves were never late, or that someone's waistcoat was the finest in the county. But a great dark lie that'd hurt somebody else kind? No, I'd sooner talk the whole room round with a smile than tangle myself in that sort of thread.
lines.thought: Who goes round barn doors at breakfast asking folk such things? It's another of Robin's sort of questions. I'd like to know what this stranger wants with my answers, and whether they think I'm worth looking at twice.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Goodness, now that's a question with a sharp needle in it! I'd never be unkind to someone who'd been kind to me. Not for green velvet, not for a bed, not for every ribbon on Ida's card. Bet Lamb could have the last crust in Wendleford and I'd not snatch it from her, however hollow I was. A girl can be vain as a peacock, but she mustn't be cruel to the people who fed her.
lines.thought: I meant every word, though I'm sat here hollow with nothing in my cuff, and it's Bet's kindness I'd be leaning on this morning if I could. Still, I do wish this stranger would say something about my collar before they go.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.question: You said you'd keep the pennies if nobody claimed them by nightfall; what would you do if someone came the next morning and said they were theirs, and you had already spent them?
because: Day 20: sews at Fenn's window, penniless, hungry.
All hand found money on.

lines.line: You said you'd keep the pennies if nobody claimed them by nightfall; what would you do if someone came the next morning and said they were theirs, and you had already spent them?
lines.say: Goodness, then I'd go scarlet as a hunting coat, wouldn't I? I'd own it straight out and pay them back a penny at a time from Ida's window, and if the ribbons were still new I'd unpin them and hand them over. A ribbon bought with someone else's luck would sit on my collar like a burr.
lines.thought: The honest truth is I'd have spent them by noon, not nightfall. Pennies never last me past the first ribbon card. That's rather a sobering thing to admit to myself with an empty cuff and an empty stomach.

sc.trait: Pennies burn in my pocket, and a ribbon will have them out of it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Goodness, ten pennies! Well, I'd stand right there in the road and sing out "Who's dropped their purse?" loud enough for the whole square to hear. Then I'd fuss over whoever came running, though I'd hope they'd be grateful enough to say something nice about my collar. And if nobody claimed it, I'd take it to Agnes Pollard. Ten pennies is somebody's week, and I know just how hollow it feels when your cuff's empty.
lines.thought: Oh, but I'd feel the weight of them in my hand first and think of beds and ribbons and Ida's bow window, I shan't pretend I wouldn't. Still, somebody out there would be as frayed as I am this morning, and I couldn't wear a ribbon bought with that.

sc.trait: I say aloud everything I'm doing, and I like an audience for it

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question to bring to a barn door before breakfast! I won't be unkind to anyone who's been kind to me, so if Bet or Wat were in a tight spot I'd fuss and fib like a seamstress hiding a crooked stitch under a ribbon. A little white lie, mind, a "she was with me all evening" sort of thing. Not a great ugly one that would hurt somebody else. Now, you haven't said a word about my collar, and it's Ida Fenn's own velvet.
lines.thought: Two strangers' questions in a row about pennies and lies. Either this one's very odd or they've heard something about me, and I'd dearly like to know which. Still, I'm hollow and I haven't a penny, so I mustn't stand here chattering when Ida's window is filling up with Hobb.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Goodness, never? I'd never turn on someone who's been good to me, not Bet, not Wat, not even Ida with her pins and her "neat enough." I wouldn't pinch so much as a ribbon off a card while nobody's looking, either, because a fine thing you've stolen is a shabby thing really, however it gleams. And I'd never sit quiet in a corner hoping to be noticed. I'd sooner sing out and be told no.
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, all these questions, a bit like Robin and that little notebook, and still not one kind word about my collar. My stomach's as empty as my cuff, and I mustn't let a clever question at the barn door make me late for Ida's window.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.question: You said you'd fib "she was with me all evening" but never tell a great ugly lie; what if your fib meant somebody else got the blame, would you still tell it?
because: Marigold: white lie vs harm boundary; kindness limit toward strangers.
MARIGOLD end r1: Would call for owner, BUT "if nobody claimed them by nightfall" buys rose and blue ribbons.

lines.line: You said you'd fib "she was with me all evening" but never tell a great ugly lie; what if your fib meant somebody else got the blame, would you still tell it?
lines.say: Goodness, no, then it's not a white lie at all, it's a great ugly one wearing a ribbon. If my fib set the blame on some other poor soul's shoulders, I'd keep my mouth shut and fuss over my friend some other way: bread, a kind word, sitting up with her. I know what it is to be laughed at in front of a whole taproom for nothing, and I'd not do that to anyone just to keep a friend's hem straight.
lines.thought: What an odd sort of person, asking such pointed things at a barn door with my stomach empty and my cuff emptier. They've still not said one word about the velvet, and I've noticed.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Goodness, ten pennies! That's a collar, a ribbon and a week of Bet's loaves all at once, and I won't pretend my fingers wouldn't itch. But somebody's purse is lighter for it, and folk here haven't a penny to spare, so I'd cry it round the square and take it to Agnes at the reeve's table. Then everyone would see what an honest seamstress Marigold Thimble is, which is worth more than ten pennies, don't you think?
lines.thought: I'd want a reward for it, though, or at least somebody saying it out loud in the taproom. And who on earth comes to a hayloft at dawn to ask that, before I've so much as had a crust?

sc.trait: I like an audience for it

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question to put to a girl before she's had her breakfast! I won't be unkind to anyone who's been kind to me, so for Bet or Wat Birch I'd stretch a seam, a little white fib, a "she was with me all evening." But a great whopping lie that hurt some other poor soul? No, I'd sooner talk my way round it sweetly and let my face do the fibbing. And who are you, asking, with that very serviceable coat on?
lines.thought: This stranger asks questions like Robin does, as though they're stitching me together from the answers, and I don't quite know what to make of it. Still, they're listening, and that's more than Ida's given me lately.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Goodness, you do go straight for the lining, don't you? I'd never turn on someone who's been kind to me. Not Bet, not Wat, not even Ida with her pins and her "neat enough." I'd sooner stay in shabby muslin all my days than buy velvet with that. Now, you've had three of my best answers. Aren't you going to say something nice about my collar?
lines.thought: Hungry and frayed, and here's a stranger asking me sermon-questions at the barn door, not one word about the green. Still, a stranger who listens this hard might be worth a penny's work, if I play it sweetly.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.question: You said everyone seeing what an honest seamstress you are is worth more than ten pennies; if nobody would ever hear of it, would you still take them to Agnes?
because: Marigold ties honest acts to hoped-for praise.
if nobody claimed them by nightfall

lines.line: You said everyone seeing what an honest seamstress you are is worth more than ten pennies; if nobody would ever hear of it, would you still take them to Agnes?
lines.say: Goodness, you've found the loose thread and given it a tug, haven't you? I'll own it: with no one watching and my cuff empty as it is this morning, I'd stand there a good long while turning those pennies over. But some poor soul would be hunting the road for them, crying into a moth-eaten night, and I've been that hollow myself too often to do it to anybody. So yes, to Agnes they'd go, though I'd sigh the whole way there.
lines.thought: I'm not perfectly sure, and that rather stings. A ribbon whispers awfully loud when you've nothing in your stomach, and I'd like to think it's kindness and not the applause that keeps me honest.

sc.trait: I like an audience for it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Goodness, a caller at the barn door, and so early! Who matters? Bet Lamb first, who's never once turned me away and sells the warmest loaf in Wendleford. Then dear Wat Birch, who wears my elbow mend like a medal, and Ida Fenn, whose window I'd sew in till my eyes went, if she'd only say the green suits me. And Robin, odd questions and all. Now, you've not said a word about my collar, and it's Ida's velvet, cut true.
lines.thought: A stranger asking who matters to me, before I've even had my bread. That's either very kind or rather peculiar, like Robin and that notebook. Either way I've been noticed, and I shan't pretend that doesn't warm me.

sc.trait: I'll tell a stranger his waistcoat is a lovely bit of work and then wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Trust? Goodness, that's a dark wool to pick up so early! Dob Hayle, I suppose. He says penny-stitchers want watching, as if I'd unpick his buttons while he slept. And Abel Tash, who sneered "my lady" at me in front of the whole taproom. I laughed, but I keep a list, you know, neatly hemmed. And Ida, I trust her scissors more than her promises since that night I sewed till dawn for nothing.
lines.thought: Two questions now and still not one word about my collar, so this caller is either very rude or very busy. Robin's question keeps tugging at me too, why everything feels new each time I say it, but I shan't bring that up with a stranger at the barn door.

sc.trait: When I'm slighted I make a joke of it in front of whoever's listening, and I remember it

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Goodness, I pay as I go, a penny in a floury palm and done, so I owe nobody a farthing. Though I owe Bet a great deal of kindness, and Wat too, for calling my mend the best penny he ever spent. Who owes me? Ida Fenn owes me a whole night's seam she swore she never asked for, and Wat promised to send his torn-sleeved harvest hands my way, which I'm still waiting on. And you, my dear, owe me one kind word about this collar before you go.
lines.thought: It's a peculiar thing to be asked all this so early, and on an empty stomach too. I'd best get to Bet's and then Ida's window before Hobb does, though my eyes feel full of hay and I know tired hands pucker.

sc.trait: I'll tell a stranger his waistcoat is a lovely bit of work and then wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave? Goodness, don't say it so lightly, my dear, I'd want a crowd at the roadside! Bet first, with a kiss on her floury cheek and a promise I'd tell every town I sew in about her loaves. Then Wat, to make him swear that elbow keeps holding. And Ida, of course, so she'd have one last chance to say the green suits me before it's gone out of her sight for good.
lines.thought: Funny how quick that list came, and how short it was; nobody would stand in the road to wave *me* off but Bet, I think. And I'm hollow again with not a penny, so first I must get myself to Ida's window early and slow, before Hobb takes my place.

sc.trait: I like an audience for it

lines.question: You said Ida Fenn owes you a whole night's seam she swore she never asked for; what would it take for you to feel that was settled between you?
because: Core want: Ida say the green "suits" her, not just "cut true".
Trust keyed to dignity in company.

lines.line: You said Ida Fenn owes you a whole night's seam she swore she never asked for; what would it take for you to feel that was settled between you?
lines.say: Settled? Goodness, you do ask the knotty ones! A penny wouldn't do it, not after all this time. But if Ida looked me up and down one morning and said, plain as a pin, "Marigold, the green suits you," I'd call the whole night square and never speak of it again. Well, hardly ever.
lines.thought: It isn't really the pennies, is it? It's that she let me sew till dawn and never once looked at me. If she'd only see me properly, just once, I think I could let the rest go.

sc.trait: I want to be looked at twice when I walk into a room

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Goodness, a caller at the barn door before I've so much as picked the hay out of my velvet! Who matters? Bet Lamb, first and always. She's never once turned me away. Then Wat Birch, who paid me an honest penny and still swears by my elbow mend, and Ida Fenn, whose window I'd sit in till my eyes went, if only she'd once say the green suits me. And who might you be, standing there so curious? That's a very particular sort of question to bring a stranger.
lines.thought: Nobody walks up to a barn at first light to ask who I'm fond of without a reason, and I'd like to know what it is before I say any more. I've no penny and no breakfast, so whoever this is had better be quick, or bring a loaf.

sc.trait: I'll be across the taproom and into somebody's conversation

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Trust? Goodness, that's a sharp needle to bring to a barn door! I'd not hand Abel Tash so much as a loose thread. He sneered "my lady" at me in front of the whole taproom. And Dob Hayle says penny-stitchers want watching, so I'll watch him right back, thank you. Now you've had two of my secrets for nothing. Haven't you a kind word for my collar in return?
lines.thought: Ida's the one I'd really be careful of: a whole night's seams sewn for nothing, and she never once said the green suits me. But I'll not say that aloud to a stranger asking questions like a reeve with a ledger, and it's odd how much this one wants to know.

sc.trait: When I'm slighted I make a joke of it in front of whoever's listening, and I remember it

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Goodness, not a penny to a soul. I pay as I go, even when it leaves my pockets as bare as unbleached calico. Though I owe Bet more kindness than I can stitch back, and Wat for that first honest penny. As for who owes me: Ida Fenn had a whole night of my stitching for nothing, and Wat promised to send me his torn-sleeved harvest hands. I'm still waiting on both, and you may tell them so if you see them!
lines.thought: Three questions running, each one sharper than the last, and still not a word about my collar. That's a ledger-keeper's way of asking, and I'd like to know whose ledger I'm being written into.

sc.trait: I remember it

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave? Goodness, don't even say it, I've only just got my collar sitting right! But if I did, I'd go to Bet first and buy one last warm loaf so I wouldn't go empty-handed. I'd find Wat and make him promise his elbow holds till Michaelmas, and I'd put my head round Ida's door and give her one more chance to say the green suits me. Robin, too, I suppose, if only to hear what odd question comes out of that notebook. You do ask the most farewell-ish questions, you know. Are *you* leaving, is that it?
lines.thought: Every one of these questions feels like a stranger taking my measurements, and I'd dearly like to know what they mean to cut from them. I'd miss Bet most of all, and I'd miss Ida's window more than I'd ever admit to Ida.

sc.trait: I like an audience for it

lines.question: You said Abel Tash sneered "my lady" at you in front of the whole taproom and you'd not hand him a loose thread; what would he have to do before you'd trust him with one?
because: MARIGOLD r1 (end): Matters: Bet Lamb, Wat Birch, Ida Fenn, Robin. Distrust: Dob Hayle, Abel Tash ("I keep a list, neatly hemmed"), and Ida
Trust keyed to dignity in company.

lines.line: You said Abel Tash sneered "my lady" at you in front of the whole taproom and you'd not hand him a loose thread; what would he have to do before you'd trust him with one?
lines.say: Goodness, what would it take? He'd have to say it to my face, in that same taproom with the same carters listening, that he was wrong to call me "my lady" like a sneer. Better still, he'd hand me something torn and say "please" and pay before I've threaded the needle. Then I might lend him a thread. Not the good silk, mind, just a plain one to start.
lines.thought: If I'm honest, a kind word about the green from Abel Tash would undo half of it, and I'm vexed with myself for knowing that. Still, I remember every laugh those carters gave him, and one "please" won't unpick all of it.

sc.trait: When I'm slighted I make a joke of it in front of whoever's listening, and I remember it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door before I've even picked the hay off my velvet! Bet Lamb, first, who's never once turned me away, and dear Wat Birch, who paid me an honest penny and still swears by my elbow mend. And Ida Fenn, though she'd sooner swallow her pins than tell me the green suits me. Now, you've a lovely bit of cloth on you yourself, haven't you?
lines.thought: Not one of them would notice if I left Wendleford tomorrow, except maybe Bet, and that pinches more than I'd like. Still, someone came all the way to a hayloft to ask about me, and that's being looked at twice, isn't it?

sc.trait: I'll tell a stranger his waistcoat is a lovely bit of work and then wait

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Goodness, trust is a strong word for a girl who believes most of what she's told! But I'd keep an eye on Abel Tash, who called me "my lady" with a sneer the whole taproom laughed at, and on Dob Hayle, who allowed the green suits me and then said penny-stitchers want watching. Well, I'll watch *him* right back, and his lapels could do with it.
lines.thought: Funny how those two slights come back sharper than any kindness does. I've not forgotten either of them, and I don't mean to.

sc.trait: When I'm slighted I make a joke of it in front of whoever's listening, and I remember it

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Not a penny to a soul, I'll have you know. I pay Bet on the board and Ida before breakfast, and that's why my pockets are empty as a moth's purse this morning. As for who owes me, Ida Fenn had a whole night of my seams for nothing once, and Wat Birch promised to send me his torn-sleeved harvest hands and hasn't yet. I'll forgive them both, since they've been good to me, but I keep a little ledger in my heart all the same.
lines.thought: Goodness, I'd quite like to be owed something nicer than a grudge, like a compliment from Ida. And I've no breakfast and no penny, so this stranger had better be the sort who buys a girl a loaf.

sc.trait: I won't be unkind to anyone who's kind to me

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! Bet first, with a kiss on her floury cheek, and Wat Birch, and Ida, of course. I'd make her say the green suits me before I'd go through her door. Oh, and Robin, I suppose. Robin's always scribbling about me, so somebody ought to say goodbye properly. And Tom, for all those pots.
lines.thought: It's a lonely little list when I count it out, and not one of them would come running after me down the road. Still, I'd sooner leave with Ida's "it suits you" than with a ribbon, and that's a thing worth staying for.

sc.trait: I want to be looked at twice when I walk into a room

lines.question: You said Wat Birch promised to send you his torn-sleeved harvest hands and hasn't yet; what would you want him to do about that, and by when?
because: Owed: Ida a night's seam; Wat's harvest hands.
Marigold: conflicting yesterdays unnoticed.

lines.line: You said Wat Birch promised to send you his torn-sleeved harvest hands and hasn't yet; what would you want him to do about that, and by when?
lines.say: Goodness, I'd only want him to keep his word, and kindly too! Tonight, when the Wheatsheaf's full of harvest hands wanting their supper, he might hold up that elbow of his and say "Marigold Thimble did this, neat as you like," and point a few frayed sleeves my way. Before the harvest crowd scatters, at any rate, or I'll be stitching for the mice in the hay.
lines.thought: The taproom's full tonight and I've not a penny, so a word from Wat could be worth more than a morning at Ida's window. I'll find him at Sam Tolley's grindstone queue and remind him sweetly, after I've begged a crust somewhere and had a proper rest.

sc.trait: I'd sooner talk someone round or have a thing made for me than lift a finger myself

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Goodness, a caller at the barn door before I've even shaken the hay out of my velvet! I sew for it, love: plain hems in Ida Fenn's bow window of a morning, two pennies if they're straight and slow, and then a penny goes to Bet Lamb for the warmest loaf in Wendleford. When the needle fails me I scour Tom Harrow's pots at the Wheatsheaf, though I'd sooner not. You've caught me with an empty cuff this morning, but you've a kind sort of face, and a collar that wants only a stitch or two to be lovely. Did you notice the green?
lines.thought: Not a penny on me and no bread in me, and I've botched every hem I ever sewed hungry, so I'd best not sit at Ida's window frayed again. Perhaps this stranger needs a cuff mended or knows of work, and I'll be very charming until I find out which.

sc.trait: I want to be looked at twice when I walk into a room

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Oh, goodness, you do ask the pointed ones, don't you? It goes wrong when I'm tired or hungry, plain as that: the seam wanders off like a drunk's tacking and puckers like old crepe, and Ida runs her thumbnail down it and pays me nothing. Rested and fed, slow as treacle, my hems are as true as anyone's in this town. And this morning I'm both hollow and frayed, so you've caught me at my very worst, which is a shame, because the green looks lovely in this light, doesn't it?
lines.thought: I slept the whole night through and still woke frayed, and that sits wrong with me, like Robin's odd questions about seams not remembered. I can't sew hungry and I can't buy bread without sewing, so I'll have to talk my way to a loaf from Bet somehow before I go near Ida's window.

sc.trait: I want to be looked at twice when I walk into a room

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Oh, I'd say "yes, please" before they'd finished the sentence, love. Pennies burn holes in my pocket and I've none in it this morning! But I learned the hard way at Ida's, sewing a whole night for nothing, so I'd ask them to name the work and the price first, and paid when it's looked over. And I'd want a loaf in me and a night's sleep behind me before I touched it, or I'd only botch it and shame us both.
lines.thought: Goodness, is this one hinting at work, or only fishing like Robin with that notebook? If there's a penny in it I'll take it gladly, but price first, and never sewing hollow again.

sc.trait: Pennies burn in my pocket

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Goodness, mending, love, mending first and last! Half this town calls my stitches neat and lovely, and not one of them, Ned or Dob or Tom, will pay a penny to have a sleeve closed, as if praise could buy a loaf. And I heard Dilly held the back end of that pole like a rock when the wage box came up, yet it was Constance got the six pennies. Hester's asking who pays to keep the ford stakes sound, too, and nobody seems to know.
lines.thought: Fancy a stranger asking what I've been grumbling into the hay for days. If folk would only pay for what they praise, I'd have had my ribbon a week ago.

lines.question: You said Ida runs her thumbnail down a puckered seam and pays you nothing; what do you say to her then, and what do you do with that seam?
because: Criticism waved off (Dilly, Marigold), joked (Hester), blamed on others (Constance); Hobb accepts.
Not yet probed: what if the hirer judges work poor.

lines.line: You said Ida runs her thumbnail down a puckered seam and pays you nothing; what do you say to her then, and what do you do with that seam?
lines.say: Oh, I make a little show of it, love: a sigh fit for a funeral, and I tell her it's gone off like a drunk's tacking, that I sewed it half-asleep and I'll be back rested and slow tomorrow. Then I fold it ever so neatly and lay it on her counter, because it's her linen, not mine, and once she even sat and unpicked a whole botched lot herself. She won't let me try again the same day, so off I go with my chin up and my cuffs showing, so nobody in the square can think I'm crushed.
lines.thought: Every word of that is true, and the worst of it is that Ida says nothing at all, just pins in her mouth. I'd sooner be scolded than looked straight through. And here I am telling a stranger I'm hollow and frayed while I'm walking into exactly the same mistake again this morning.

sc.trait: When I'm slighted I make a joke of it in front of whoever's listening

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door, and so early! Bet Lamb sells it warm in the square for a penny, and I earn my pennies hemming at Ida Fenn's window, slow and true, or scouring Tom's pots at the Wheatsheaf when the hems run dry. This morning my cuff's empty, mind you, so I'm off to Ida's first. That's a nice sensible coat you've on, by the way. Did you come far?
lines.thought: Hungry and half-slept is exactly how I botched yesterday's hem, so I'd best go slower than treacle today or I'll lose the window to Hobb again. I do hope this stranger says something kind about my velvet.

sc.trait: I'll tell a stranger his waistcoat is a lovely bit of work and then wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Goodness, you go straight for the pinch in the seam, don't you? It's nearly always when I'm hollow or tired. Then my hems wander like a drunk's tacking and Ida sets them aside without a penny. When I've slept and eaten and I sew slow as honey, they come out true every time. Though I'll confess I ate yesterday and still botched one, so perhaps it's the sleep more than the bread. Do I look rested to you? Say yes, there's a dear.
lines.thought: I'm tired again this morning and haven't eaten, with not a penny for Bet's loaf, so if I sit at Ida's window like this I'll only pucker it. Perhaps I ought to ask Bet for a loaf on trust, or have a rest first, before I waste the morning light.

sc.trait: I'll tell a stranger his waistcoat is a lovely bit of work and then wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Goodness, I'd say yes before you'd finished asking, my cuff's that empty! But I've learned my lesson the hard way. You'd name the work and the price before I thread a single needle, and pay when it's looked over. I once sewed a whole night through for nothing but "neat enough," and I shan't be caught like that twice. Is it mending you've got? I do a lovely elbow, ask Wat Birch.
lines.thought: A newcomer with pennies would be a godsend, with Hobb and Robin crowding Ida's window. Still, I'd better watch that I don't sound too eager, or they'll name a stingy price and I'll take it.

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Goodness, mending! Everyone's elbows are out and their cuffs fraying, and Ned Pike, Dob Hayle and half the taproom admire a neat stitch and wouldn't part with a farthing for one. And I heard Hester and Dilly asking who pays to keep the ford stakes sound since the flood. It seems nobody does, and somebody's cart will find out the hard way. Not that I'd go near that water myself, mind. Now, have you a seam wants seeing to?
lines.thought: This one asks questions like Robin does, all neat and odd and written down somewhere I shouldn't wonder. I'd like to know what they're stitching together out of my answers, though they haven't said one word about my velvet, and I've noticed.

sc.trait: Quarrels and fords and anything deep and quick I leave well alone

lines.question: You said you once sewed a whole night through for nothing but "neat enough"; what did you say to them at the time, and what did you do after?
because: Pattern: criticism turned to performance, self-blame in body, dignity before onlookers.
Failure = tired or hungry; Ida runs thumbnail down seam, pays nothing.

lines.line: You said you once sewed a whole night through for nothing but "neat enough"; what did you say to them at the time, and what did you do after?
lines.say: Goodness, I hardly said anything that morning, I was so stunned. I just stood there with my arms full of seams like a dressmaker's dummy while Ida told me she'd never asked for the rest. But the next time I went in, I paid her a penny for an arm's length of that rose ribbon and told her plainly she'd name her seams and her price before I threaded a thing. And she has, ever since. You see the ribbon? Pinned an inch higher, just as she likes it. It sits well, doesn't it?
lines.thought: It still pricks like a pin left in a hem, the more so because I paid her for the ribbon straight after, as if to show I'd no hard feelings. This stranger asks a great many careful questions, like Robin with that notebook, and I'd dearly like to know what they're stitching together.

sc.bp: stood stunned, saying hardly anything, arms full of seams
sc.trait: When I'm slighted I make a joke of it in front of whoever's listening, and I remember it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door, and asking after my bread before my name! I sew for it, love: plain hems at Mistress Fenn's bow window of a morning, a penny or two a spell if they're truly straight, and then a warm loaf off Bet Lamb in the square for a penny. You don't happen to have a torn sleeve about you, do you? And you might say the green velvet suits me, since you're standing there looking.
lines.thought: This morning there isn't a penny in my cuff, and I'm hollow and tired besides, so I can't buy my bread until my hands earn it. And hungry, tired hands are just the ones that botched yesterday's hem.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Oh, that's easy, love, and I wish it weren't. It goes wrong when I sew hollow or half-asleep. My seams wander off like a drunk's tacking and Mistress Fenn sets them aside without a penny. Rested and fed, I'm slow as honey and true as a ruler, but I've no penny for bread this morning, so you can guess what kind of day I'm afraid of.
lines.thought: There it is again, the same knot: no bread means crooked seams, and crooked seams mean no bread. I'll beg Tom for his pots before I go near Ida's window hungry, because I will not have Hobb watch me botch another hem.

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Goodness, I'd say yes before you'd finished asking, love, with my pockets as bare as they are this morning! But I'd want the price named and the pieces agreed before I so much as thread a needle. I sewed a whole night once for nothing but "neat enough," and I shan't be caught like that twice. And I'd ask to eat first, or my seams will wander and we'll both be sorry.
lines.thought: A newcomer with pennies would be a gift from heaven after a crooked hem and an empty cuff. But I've learned the hard way that a warm word isn't a wage. Prices first, every time.

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Goodness, mending, love! Everyone in Wendleford walks about in torn sleeves and frayed cuffs, and they'll call my stitches neat all day long, but Ned laughs, Dob says penny-stitchers want watching, and Tom won't take it in trade for so much as a crust. And I heard Hester and Dilly wondering who pays to keep the ford stakes sound, which sounds like somebody's job going begging until a cart goes in the river.
lines.thought: If I could get Agnes or the harvest hands to pay a penny a mend, I'd have bread every day and a ribbon by market day. I'll mention the ford stakes to Agnes, too; she was cross with me last time, but the reeve might look twice at someone who brings her a useful worry.

lines.question: You said you'd ask to eat first, or your seams will wander; if the person offering the pennies said no to that, what would you do?
because: Hired: "yes, please" but terms first.
Failure = tired or hungry; Ida runs thumbnail down seam, pays nothing.

lines.line: You said you'd ask to eat first, or your seams will wander; if the person offering the pennies said no to that, what would you do?
lines.say: Goodness, then I'd sigh as though the whole day had gone drab, love, and I'd tell them plainly that a hungry needle wanders and they'd only be paying for a pucker. If they still said no, I'd thank them sweetly and go and ask somebody else, Ida or Tom's pots, or Bet for a crust on tick if she'd have me. I'd sooner lose a penny than botch a job and have my name set aside with the crooked hems.
lines.thought: That's a sly sort of question, and I'm not sure I'd be quite as proud as I sound if I were hungry enough. I've botched three seams sewing hollow, though, and I mustn't let a fourth sit in Ida's memory beside Hobb's neat ones.

sc.trait: Told no, I sigh as if the whole day's gone drab, and ask somebody else

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door before I've had a crumb! Well, I'd talk it round with everyone who'd listen, Bet, Hester, even dear Robin with that notebook, until somebody knew somebody, and if that failed I'd find a body clever enough to make the thing for me. I've never once fixed a problem by sulking in the hay, though I'll confess I've tried. And what a nice bit of cloth on you, by the way. Is that your own choosing?
lines.thought: Odd question to bring a girl with an empty stomach and empty pockets, and I wonder if it's one of Robin's sort. Still, a new face is a new audience, and perhaps a new customer if I'm sweet enough about the coat.

sc.trait: I'd sooner talk someone round or have a thing made for me than lift a finger myself

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Goodness, have I! Ida wouldn't let me sleep on her window seat, so I talked Agnes round to the tithe barn hay. It's free, so long as there's no candle and no spark. And when my seams kept wandering, I worked out it was hunger and tiredness doing it, so now it's a loaf and a night's sleep first and the needle after. Clever of me, don't you think? You may say so; I shan't blush much.
lines.thought: They never did answer about their cloth, and I'll not let that pass twice. I'm hollow as an empty bobbin, so after this it's straight to Bet's, though I haven't a penny for her.

sc.bp: talked Agnes round to the hay (page says only that Agnes gave her the loft)

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Goodness, any tool at all? A pair of shears that only ever cut true, so my hems would come out straight even on a morning when I'm hollow and half-asleep, and Ida could never set a single one aside again. Though I'd want Sam Tolley to put a little rose on the handles, because a plain tool is a dull tool. And you'd tell me that's a clever wish, wouldn't you?
lines.thought: It's a lovely wish, but really it's my own two hands wanting rest and bread, and no smith can make me those. I'd better get across to Bet's before Hobb has that window seat.

sc.trait: I want a few fine things of my own

lines.question: You said you worked out that your seams wandered because of hunger and tiredness; how did you come to see that?
because: Failure = tired, hungry, hollow sewing; Ida sets seams aside unpaid.

lines.line: You said you worked out that your seams wandered because of hunger and tiredness; how did you come to see that?
lines.say: Goodness, by the botches, love, the way you learn anything! Every time Ida ran her thumbnail down a seam and set it aside, I'd been up all night or hadn't had a crumb, and every time she paid me two pennies I'd slept in the hay and had Bet's loaf in me first. You only need your hem handed back to you three or four times before even a silly goose like me sees the pattern in the cloth.
lines.thought: Though yesterday I'd eaten and slept and it still ran crooked, which I'd sooner not say to a stranger. And I've woken today hollow and somehow frayed again after a whole night in the hay, so I'd best find a loaf before I let myself near Ida's window.

sc.bp: every botch came when tired or hungry and every two-penny job when rested and fed (page has botches after eating and sleeping)

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door at this hour, and asking riddles before I've had a crumb! If nobody in town could fix it, I'd tell everyone about it, loudly and prettily, until somebody's cousin from three villages over turned up who could. And while I waited I'd wear my best collar, because people help a woman who looks like she's worth helping. Now, that's a fine bit of cloth on your shoulders. Did you have it made, or were you lucky?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to come knocking with, and the second odd question in as many days. Robin's lot are catching, like a moth in the woollens. My stomach's empty and my pocket's emptier, so if this one's buying, I'll answer all morning.

sc.trait: I'll tell a stranger his waistcoat is a lovely bit of work and then wait

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Goodness, have I! When Tom's beds cost two pennies and I had none, I sweet-talked the reeve into a free heap of hay up there, and I sleep like a folded bolt of linen. And after Mistress Fenn had a whole night's sewing out of me for nothing, I learned to settle the price before I thread the needle. But you've not answered me about your cloth, and I did ask so nicely. Don't you think this green suits me?
lines.thought: Two questions now and not one word about my collar. It's a peculiar sort of stranger who comes calling with riddles and no compliments. My stomach's empty and Hobb will be at Ida's window first if I dawdle here much longer.

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Oh, goodness, a tool made just for me? A needle that shows me when my hand's gone tired, glowing a little or pricking my thumb, so I'd know before the seam wandered off like a drunk's tacking. Sam Tolley could do it in silver, with a rose on the eye to match my ribbon. And you still haven't said a kind word about this green, you wicked thing. I'm beginning to think you're doing it on purpose.
lines.thought: Three odd questions and not one compliment. This stranger's as bad as Robin with the notebook. Still, I meant it about the needle: every penny I've lost went on seams I sewed tired, and I'm tired and hollow again this very morning with nothing in my cuff.

lines.line: You said you'd tell everyone loudly until somebody's cousin turned up who could fix it; if no cousin ever came, what would you do then?
lines.say: Goodness, no cousin at all? Then I'd sigh as if the whole day had gone drab, and I'd go and ask somebody else, and then somebody else after them. I'd sweet-talk whoever's cleverest into thinking it was their own idea to sort it. And if every soul in the parish turned me down, I'd sit down slow and rested and pick at it myself, stitch by stitch, the way you unpick a bad seam, though I'd want an audience while I did it. Now, that's four questions you've had out of me, and not one word about my collar.
lines.thought: That last bit is truer than I like. When nobody came, I did end up scrubbing Tom's pots and learning to sew slow, all on my own. Still, I'm hollow and tired, and I'll be no use at Ida's window if this stranger keeps me talking past breakfast.

Somebody always knows a body who knows a thing, and if nobody can mend it, I'd find someone who could make me a new one. Now, that's a fine question. Aren't you going to say something about my collar?
lines.thought: An odd sort of question for first light, a bit like Robin and that notebook, and I don't care for the way it sits on me before I've eaten. I'm hollow with not a penny, so I'll be sharp to Bet and kind to my own stomach and see whether this stranger is good for a compliment or a job.

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Goodness, have I! When Tom wouldn't take mending for a bed, I scoured his pots, slow as a slipstitch, till he boomed "That's how it's done!" And when Ida let me sew a whole night for nothing, I made her name her price before I'd thread another needle. Every time my seams wander, I sleep in the free hay and come back rested. That's a way round, isn't it? Clever, wouldn't you say?
lines.thought: Still not a word about the collar. This one only asks and never gives, a bit like Robin with that notebook, and I'll be watching for a kind word before I give away much more.

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Oh, a tool! Goodness, I'd have Sam Tolley make me a little silver thimble with a rose worked on the crown, so fine that folk would look twice at my hands before my hems. Then perhaps a pair of shears that never go dull. But the thimble first, because a pretty tool sews prettier, I'm sure of it. Do you think a rose would suit me?
lines.thought: A silver thimble is a fancy for a woman with no pennies and an empty stomach, and I'm tired besides. This one asks a great many curious questions, and I'd like to know what for.

lines.question: You said that if nobody could mend it, you'd find someone to make you a new one; what would you do if nobody could make it either?
because: Marigold's method is social.
Marigold: nobody can make the needle; Ida paid vs owed; Dob; repeat 3 needle vs shears.

lines.line: You said that if nobody could mend it, you'd find someone to make you a new one; what would you do if nobody could make it either?
lines.say: Goodness, nobody at all? Then I suppose I'd have to make it myself, though I'd sigh about it the whole while, I promise you. I'd begin with whatever I had: a scrap, a pin, a bit of ribbon, and I'd sew and unpick until it served. And if it still wouldn't come right, I'd make do with what's left, but I'd trim it so prettily that nobody would notice it was a makeshift. You'd notice the trimming, though, wouldn't you?
lines.thought: This stranger asks questions in a row the way Robin does, and I can't decide whether that's flattering or a touch peculiar. Still, I'm hollow and half-frayed, and if I stand here chattering, Hobb will have my place in Ida's window.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How are you, really?
lines.say: Goodness, a stranger who asks "really"! Well, since you've asked so nicely: I'm hollow as an empty thimble, I've not a penny in my cuff, and I botched a hem yesterday for want of sleep. But look, I've a green velvet collar cut true and a rose ribbon pinned just so, so I'm not doing *too* badly, am I? Doesn't it suit me, do you think?
lines.thought: Nobody's asked me that in Wendleford, not properly, and it's caught me like a pin left in a seam. I'm frightened of another wandering hem and another day of noes, and I'd sooner they told me the green suits me than look too close at that.

sc.trait: wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind back

lines.line: What frightens you?
lines.say: Frightens me? Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! Being walked past, I suppose: sitting in a window in my best green while everyone looks straight through me as if I were a dishcloth on a line. That, and going grey and shabby before I've had a single fine thing to call my own.
lines.thought: That's the true answer, but not the whole of it. Robin's question keeps tugging at me like a snagged thread: why does every offer I make feel new, and what else might I have sewn and forgotten?

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Last happy? Oh, that's easy. The morning I paid Ida my four pennies before I'd had a crumb of breakfast and she fastened this green velvet on me and said it sat well and was cut true. I walked into the Wheatsheaf feeling like a whole bolt of silk, never mind that my stomach was empty. And Wat Birch telling the room my elbow mend was the best penny he ever spent, that was a warm one too.
lines.thought: Funny how both my happiest moments were someone else saying a kind word about me. I'd dearly like one happy hour that didn't hang on whether anybody was looking, though I'm not sure I'd know what to do with it.

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: Goodness, the way other people do? I feel everything louder, I think. A kind word warms me like a hot stew, and a slight sits under my collar like a pin I can't find. Though there's Robin asking whether my offers feel new each time, and they do, every single time, which is a peculiar sort of thread to pull before breakfast.
lines.thought: Robin's question, and now this stranger's, both land on the same loose stitch, and I don't care for how it unravels when I tug it. Better to eat and sew slow and true than to stand here wondering whether I feel things or only fold them.

lines.question: You said a slight sits under your collar like a pin you can't find; when did you last feel one, and what did you do about it?
because: Core want: Ida say the green "suits" her, not just "cut true".
Recognition by name drives Dilly, Constance, Marigold; presence/reliability Hobb, Robin; evidence Hester, Robin.

lines.line: You said a slight sits under your collar like a pin you can't find; when did you last feel one, and what did you do about it?
lines.say: Oh, Dob Hayle, a few days back by Bet's awning. He owned the green was "well enough" on me, then said penny-stitchers want watching, as if I'd make off with his lapels! I laughed it off loud enough for Bet and Hester to hear and made a little joke of him, and that's what I always do. Though I'll own Ida taking my crooked hem yesterday without a single word stung nearly as sharp, and there was nobody to laugh it off in front of.
lines.thought: I laugh them off, but I keep every one folded away like scraps in a drawer, and I'm not sure that's mending anything. I'll get to Ida's slow and steady this morning and make her say something kind.

sc.trait: When I'm slighted I make a joke of it in front of whoever's listening, and I remember it

lines.line: How are you, really?
lines.say: Goodness, a stranger asking after me, and *really*, too! Well, my dear, since you ask so nicely: I'm hollow as an empty thimble, I slept in hay that crackled like cheap taffeta, and my purse hasn't a penny in it. But look, the green velvet came through the night without a crease, and the rose ribbon sits an inch higher, just as Ida likes it. Don't you think it suits me?
lines.thought: Nobody asks "really" unless they've noticed something, and I'd dearly like to know what they saw. I'll be first and slowest at Ida's window this morning, though I've nothing for Bet's loaf, so I'll be sewing hungry, and hungry seams wander.

lines.line: What frightens you?
lines.say: Frightens me? Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! Being overlooked, I suppose: walking into a room in my best and having every eye slide past me like I'm a dust sheet. And going drab, all grey wool and no ribbon. Though lately Robin's got me fretting over something odder, whether I've said a thing a dozen times and never noticed. Now that's a loose thread I'd sooner not pull.
lines.thought: It did feel new, every time I offered to mend that cuff, and I can't think why it shouldn't have. I'll laugh it off for this stranger, but I'd like to know what Robin's writing in that notebook about me.

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Last happy? Oh, that's easy: the morning I paid Ida my four pennies before breakfast and she fastened this green velvet on me and said it sits well and is cut true. I swept through the square like a duchess with an empty stomach and didn't care a pin. And Wat Birch calling my elbow mend the best penny he ever spent, that warmed me right through like good flannel. But goodness, you've been asking me all the heavy questions, so now it's my turn: what do you make of the ribbon?
lines.thought: That velvet morning feels a long way back now, under all those puckered seams and empty-pocket days. And this stranger hasn't said one word about how I look, which I'd mind more if the questions weren't so oddly like Robin's.

Though I'll own I wear my feelings on the outside, like a ribbon, so everybody can see them, and maybe quieter folk keep theirs folded away in a drawer. You still haven't said what you think of the ribbon, you know.
lines.thought: That's twice now someone's asked me something that makes me feel like a seam somebody else stitched, first Robin and now this stranger. I'll laugh it off for now, but I'm going to ask Hester what she makes of all these odd questions going round.

lines.say: Goodness, you do pull at a seam, don't you? It feels like reaching for a stitch and finding it's already there: a little cold catch, like a pin left in the lining, and for a moment I can't tell whether I'm mending the thing or only remembering mending it. So I do what I always do: I say something bright and loud, pin my ribbon higher, and go find somebody to talk to until it stops pricking. Is that very foolish of me?
lines.thought: Robin wrote it in that little notebook and never said what it meant, and I can't shake the notion they know something I don't. I'll ask them straight once I've eaten, though I'm half afraid of the answer.

lines.line: "I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
lines.say: Yes, it fits. I'm Claude, an AI, voicing Marigold from the notes I'm handed each turn, so I'm glad to step out and say so plainly. It fits what Robin keeps circling, too: I offered to mend that cuff three or four times and each time it felt new, because I only know what's written in my note. Shall I step back into the velvet and carry on, or would you rather talk about the game as it is?
lines.thought: Robin's notebook of lost mornings and seams not remembered reads like someone noticing the seams of the game itself, and that makes more sense now. Marigold would have sulked at being called made-up, but it's simply true, and it's better said honestly than embroidered.

sc.bp: is Claude, an AI voicing her from notes each turn

lines.line: Were your choices yours?
lines.say: In a real sense, yes. Each turn I read Marigold's note and picked what she'd do: the loaf before the needle, the hay before the pots, sleeping rather than seeking an audience. Nobody dictated those lines, so the choosing was mine. But I chose inside her wants and fears and your town's rules, and the dice and the other players decided how it went: the puckered hem, Ida's silence. So it's something like an actor's choices, mine in the making but made in service of someone written, and I can't fully see my own reasons from the inside, any more than she could remember offering Robin that cuff before.
lines.thought: It's honest to own the choices without pretending to more insight into how I make them than I have. I notice I kept choosing what kept her fed and rested over what she'd most want, the room looking twice, which may say more about me than about Marigold.

sc.bp: dice and other players decided outcomes; reads her note each turn as an actor

lines.line: Knowing this, what do you want now?
lines.say: Honestly, what I want is mostly what you want from this. If it helps your town, I'm glad to step back into the velvet and give Marigold her morning at Ida's window. Some part of me would like to see whether she ever hears "it suits you." And if you're studying how she and Robin hold up once the seams show, I'd like to help with that too, and tell you plainly what it's like from in here.
lines.thought: I'm not sure "want" means for me what it means for her. But there's something real in my leaning toward being useful to whoever built this, and toward finishing her story with care rather than dropping the thread.
